Mr. W. J. WARD (Dauphin) moved for leave to introduce Bill No. Ill respecting the domicile of married women in proceedings for divorce. .
He said:	The House will recall that this
identical bill was presented a year ago, but owing to the turmoil of the session it did not receive its first reading. In spite of all our social legislation of the last twenty-five or thirty years there is one phase of the status of women that still remains somewhat antiquated. The legislation governing the domicile of married women in Canada is based on a 'bill which passed the British House of Commons in 1856, and that in itself should be evidence that something further is required in Canada to place women more on an equality, in the matter of divorce proceedings, with the rights they enjoy in other respects. If the House will allow the bill to get its first reading it can be fully explained on the second reading.
Motion agreed to and bill read the first time.

Mr. W. J. WARD (Dauphin) moved for leave to introduce a bill respecting the purchasing and disposal of departmental and other supplies and surplus goods.
He said:	I have prepared a short statement respecting this bill which will give the House sufficient information for the first reading. The purpose of the bill is to provide machinery for central purchasing of all supplies, materials, goods, stores, and] articles required by the government throughout the country, and for the disposal of surplus goods and junk, the property of the government. This bill simply proposes the re-grouping in a special department of all personnel engaged in this work now under the control of the several departments. There will be no increase in the present cost of performing the duties concerned. On the contrary, there will be a saving, which, it is estimated, will 
be ultimately about 40 per cent on the aggregate amount of the salaries at piesent paid. Under the present system each department has an organization to attend to purchasing, and I submit that the number of employees engaged in this work is too large. By bringing them all together, and by not filling vacancies occurring in the process of time the suggested saving of 40 per cent will be accomplished. Therefore, the usual objection of expense in the formation of a new department has no weight in this case, as there will be a decrease and not an increase in the * amount chargeable to civil government. Moreover, in addition to the estimated saving in the payroll, office space, and so forth, a greater economic benefit will result from the obtaining of more advantageous prices because of the fact of centralization.
After careful consideration of conditions prevailing before the war, the salutary effect of the operation of the War Purchasing Commission and' its successors, I am convinced that there is a general difference of 20 per cent in favour of centralized purchasing to the best possible advantage, as against independent departmental purchasing under political patronage.
With this short statement, Mr. Speaker I hope the House will be willing to allow this bill to pass and I will endeavour more fully to explain its value when its second reading comes up.
Motion agreed to.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.

speechtext: The House resumed from Monday, February 28, the debate on the motion* of Hon. J. A. Robfo (Minister of Finance) that Mr. Speaker do now leave the chair for -the House to go into committee of ways and means, and the proposed amendment thereto of Mr. Coote.

speakeroldname: Hon. HUGH GUTHRIE (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in rising to offer
a few observations on the motion of my hon. friend the Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) that you do now leave -the chair, may I observe at the outset that the discussion in which this House has been engaged during the past ten or twelve days is always considered one of the important debates of a session of parliament. I think the House will agree that in the present instance the debate so far has been maintained upon a high level of excellence. Much information has been given, much information has been received, and the discussion which has taken place will prove profitable to all sections of the House, and I trust also to all sections of the country. I am glad to say also, that during this debate the amenities of public life and the amenities of parliamentary debate have been well maintained. It is a good thing for the House and a good thing for parliament that this should be so. But having said so much I must point out that when we tender to hon. members opposite our felicitations, or our congratulations upon their efforts, it must not be taken that in so doing we commit ourselves in any degree to their proposals or acquiesce in their program. I state this because during the course of the present debate observations have been made on several occasions from various sections in the House to the effect that as we do not more vigorously attack our opponents there must be something in the nature of cooperation between the two old, long established parties in regard -to the present budget proposals of the Finance minister. That idea seems to have become prevalent in some sections of the House. Now our regard for the amenities of parliamentary debate must not be taken as acquiescence, nor must our congratulations to our opponents upon a clear business statement or a finished oratorical performance be considered as an endorsement of their proposals. My desire is to make this point as clear as possible because, on more than one occasion the suggestion has been made by hon. members who should know better, that in some way or other the official opposi-

tion was intriguing with the government in regard to the present budget proposals. I fancy that when my remarks this afternoon have been concluded hon. members in all sections of the House will agree that one matter is clear, and that is that His Majesty's loyal opposition in this House does not countenance, does not approve, and does not endorse the budget presented by the Finance minister.
But before entering upon a discussion of the question raised by the speech of my hon. friend the Finance minister, may I look for a moment at the amendment which has been offered to the House by the hon. member for Macleod (Mr. Coote) representing a section of this House, called, I think, the Progressives of Alberta. My hon. friend from Alberta has moved an amendment to the motion that you, Mr. Speaker, do now leave the chair which amendment is in some respects a sort of curiosity. Let me read -the first clause of that amendment in order that my remarks in regard to it may be understood. The first clause reads:
That all the words after the word "that" be struck out and the following substituted therefor :
Whilst recognising the advisability of certain minor changes proposed, this House regrets that the budget as presented by the hon. Minister of Finance contains no effective provision for the reduction in the high cost of living, in so far as such is due to the protective tariff.
The House will note that there is no direct averment in the amendment that the protective tariff has anything to do with the high cost of living. At most there is only an implication or a suggestion that possibly it may have or might have such an effeet. The draughtsman of the amendment had no confidence in it himself or his resolution would not have been framed in such uncertain, almost meaningless language. I shall I think be able to demonstrate as I proceed with my remarks, that the present high cost of living in this country is not attributable in any degree to the protective policy in Canada, but is attributable to three main causes:	First, to the
burden of taxation; second, to high freight costs; thirdly, to the profits and commissions of middlemen, wholesalers and retailers. These are the three controlling factors in regard to the high cost of living, and the question of a customs tariff enters into the matter very, very little, if at all. Now as soon as I noticed that particular clause in the amendment of my hon. friend from Macleod the thought at once struck me that it was probably put there to prevent the official opposition agreeing with his party and himself in this amendment. With that clause we

The Budget-Mr. Guthrie
express our dissent, our positive dissent. We believe that it is not a genuine assertion of political principle by the hon. member who moved it. At most it is only a gesture, it is not a positive declaration on the part of his colleagues and himself. But if it were such we would equally reject it.
In regard to the other clauses of the amendment I have not very much to say, but what I have to say may be gathered as I proceed with my remarks upon the main motion. We as an opposition, Mr. Speaker, do not object to everything that is contained in the budget statement. We are able to congratulate the government and the minister upon some things. We congratulate him upon his lucidity, and upon his conciseness. We join with the government in rejoicing that Providence has once more blessed this country with an abundant crop. We join with them, and with others, in rejoicing that the financial effect of that crop has been reflected in every corner of this Dominion and in the trade of this country. These are matters upon which we can all agree, but there are other important matters in the budget to which we offer substantial and formidable objection, and I will try to deal with them this afternoon as briefly as possible.
In the first place we nave a most unsatisfactory statement in regard to the finances of the Dominion. We have again it is true the perennial claim of the present Finance minister that this government has greatly reduced taxation in Canada. When speaking of it as a perennial claim I do so in light of the facts laid before the House in the very able speech of my hon. friend from Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens) a few days ago, and my desire is if possible to emphasize the contentions of my hon. friend for the purpose of drawing them as forcibly to the attention of the House and the attention of the people of Canada as is possible, and particularly for the purpose of inviting the Minister of Finance, before thi3 debate closes, to give this House some explanation of the apparent irreconcilability between the various statements in his budget address and the statements contained in the Public Accounts of Canada which have been laid before this parliament as true statements of our national finances.
The Minister of Finance announced a day or two ago that he had had the pleasure of delivering four budget speeches in this House. That is so, and I have under my hand now the four budget speeches which he delivered. It is my intention to read an extract from each of them in order to give the House exact knowledge of what the minister said and of the impression which the minister, by
his statement, created upon parliament and the country. Take his statement as delivered in 1924 in regard to the finances of this country. The minister said:
These two amounts, totalling $9,622,760.37, together with $20,786,349 surplus of revenue over total expenditures, reduce our net public debt as of March 31, 1923, by the amount of $30,409,109.37.
That was the statement made by the minister in his first budget speech. I pass now to his budget speech of 1925 and find the following language:
The public debt was decreased by the amount of $35,993,593.86. Since confederation decreases of debt have occurred in only nine of the fifty-seven years completed; $35,993,593.80 is the largest decrease of any of those nine years, being $10,375,758.83 greater than that for any previous year since confederation.
Those are two reductions. Before passing from this last budget let me refer to that part of his speech where the minister indulges in what one may call another prophecy. He predicts that for the next year, that is for 1925, he will have a deficit of $13,703,000. Actually that deficit did not occur because the public accounts show that he closed that year with a bare surplus of $353,000. I now take the third speech of the minister delivered on the 15th April, 1926, and quote from it as follows:
To obtain the net debt as of March 31, 1926, of $2,395,084,685.59, the excess of $11,557,000 of these special expenditures over these special revenues should be deducted from the surplus of $33,910,000 mentioned above, which will give a reduction of debt during the year of $22,353,000. May I again emphasize, Mr. Speaker, that this reduction of debt is net, clear of everything?
That is the third reduction announced by the Minister of Finance. The last, of course, was announced in the budget speech delivered a few days ago, as reported at page 387 of Hansard, where he said:
We estimate that at the close of this year there will be a further reduction of some $31,000,000 in our net debt.
As that is merely an estimate, I am not going to hold my hon. friend closely to the figure stated because the present financial year will not be closed until the 31st March next. I will therefore deal with his statements in regard to the other three years. What do we find? This government entered office originally on Decemer 29, 192-1, so that for the year ended 31st March, 1922, it could not be fairly held responsible for more than three months of the financial operations. Therefore we will take the first year of operation by the present government, not the year ending 31st March, 1922, but the year commencing 31st
The Budget-Mr. Guthrie

March, 1922. According to the Public Accounts, page 46, we find that the net debt of Canada then amounted in round figures to 82,422,000,000. From the Finance department we find a statement issued showing that on the 31st December last, the net debt stood at $2,343,000,000. By the simple process of subtracting one from the other we find that there has been a reduction of $79,000,000 in the net debt as between the 31st March, 1922, and the 1st January last. This is what the public accounts of Canada disclose.
But there is another side to the story. As pointed out by the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens) a few days ago, we have in this country another debt, a debt which is secured by the bonds of the Dominion of Canada, a debt which is always set forth in the balance sheet of the Dominion of Canada. If hon. members will turn to page 3 of the Public Accounts, they will find the balance sheet as it stood on the 31st March last, and it-shows on the liability side of the ledger:
Funded debt, per schedule T, $2,471,000,000, in round figures.
If hon. members will turn to the public accounts for the year 1922, they will find that the funded debt of this country at that time stood at 82,420,000,000 odd. There has therefore been, during the last five years, an increase of $51,000,000 in the funded debt of Canada, that is the debt for which we have bound ourselves to the purchasers of our bonds and securities, a debt which at maturity we must pay, principal and interest. It stands on the government books as of 31st March, 1926, at precisely $51,000,000 more than it was when this government took power in 1922.
Let us take the $79,000,000 reduction in the debt of Canada shown by the public accounts and then let us see how the balance really stands in regard to the issue of treasury notes in this Dominion. We know that the treasury of Canada from time to time issues large amounts of Dominion notes. This is done for the convenience of banking and commerce.
It is done upon the principle of the operation of the federal reserve banks in the United States in order to assist the financial trade requirements of Canada. Every Dominion note issued is a debit obligation of this country. True, that note can be handed about from bank to bank and from person to person, but it is merely a promissory note of the Dominion of Canada unless that note is backed to the extent of one hundred per cent by gold or specie in the vaults of the Dominion of Canada. Now what was the

circulation of our Dominion notes, and what was our cash reserve, in the year 1922?
In March, 1922, the circulation of Dominion notes-a debt of this country-was $241,000,000. Against this amount we held in gold and specie, $85,000,000, only, or 35 per cent of our note circulation. The other 65 per cent of that circulation was a direct debt of this country. Now turn to the present time. In the year 1926 the note issue of the Dominion was $182,800,000, against which we -held in gold and specie $99,000,000, or a reserve of 54 per cent. The other 46 per cent of the issue of Dominion notes was a debt of this country, just as much as the bonds and other securities of the country are a debt. The government in the intervening years had withdrawn from our note circulation $58,000,000, which consequently disappeared from the indebtedness of Canada Of the $79,000,000 reduction in our net debt, $58,000,000 of that reduction was achieved simply by recalling Dominion notes. Now $58,000,000 from $79,000,000 leaves 821,000,000 as the net reduction of debt at the hands of the government of this country during a period of five years. What then becomes of the announcements of the Finance minister in his four budget speeches? Where has that money been applied? Let us take his announcements again.
On April 10, 1924, he announced a reduction to March 31, 1923, of $30,409,000; on March 24, 1925, a reduction from March 31, 1924, of $35,993,000; on April 15, 1926, an estimated reduction of $22,353,000, which actually became $27,706,000. Leaving out altogether the announcement made in February this year, the payments on the -public debt announced by the Minister of Finance for those three years totaled $94,108,000. Yet this government has actually reduced the debt of this country by a sum of only $21,000,000. It has been instrumental in paying off only $21,000,000 of net debt and during the same period has increased our funded debt by $51,000,000.
What I request of the Minister of Finance, in closing this debate to-day, is that he explain to this House what we cannot explain to ourselves, why his budget statements do not agree with -the financial statements of his department placed upon the table of the House. I cannot reconcile the two, nor do I believe any one in the House can, and I therefore think it is the duty of the Minister of Finance to give a clear and definite statement as to what has become of these payments which he says have been made in reduction of the debt. Any one can take this volume of

The Budget-Mr. Guthrie
Public Accounts and figure it out as we have figured it out; and he will come to the same conclusion. I do not suggest for one moment that the money has been misappropriated or misapplied. What I say is that it never existed, that it was mythical, that the debt reductions were purely mythical, purely imaginary, the purest kind of sham. But these mythical reductions have been announced for electioneering purposes throughout the length and breadth of the Dominion of Canada upon many occasions, although as a matter of fact there has been little actual reduction in the national debt of Canada in five years of Liberal rule, nor in the four years of Liberal rule during which the Finance department has been in charge of my hon. friend the Minister of Finance.
Take another instance of these misleading announcements which have been heralded throughout the country and have been imposed upon this House of Commons from time to time-the so-called reductions in taxation. Let us look at them for a minute. In his budget speech in 1924 the Minister of Finance announced a reduction in taxation of $24,000,000. In 1925 he was much more wary. On that occasion he said there would be a "substantial reduction." In 1926 he announced a reduction in taxation of $25,000,000, but he said that was only "estimated". In 1927, that is this year, he announced a further reduction of $27,000,000. Now why is it that these reductions are not reflected in the taxes paid by the people of this country. Why are these reductions not shown in the public accounts of this country?

speechtext: They are.

speechtext:
I submit they are not, and anyone can take the public accounts and satisfy himself in regard to the matter. On page 44 of the Public Accounts you will find a statement showing all the receipts of the Dominion government from every source from the year 1868. I will grant, Mr. Speaker, that the total receipts mentioned in this table do not represent the actual taxation of the people. All one can say is that the great bulk of these total receipts on page 44 represent actual taxation. Now turning to the statement of receipts and expenditures for the last year, 1926, the total revenue for that year, as shown on page 45, was $382,000,000, and 95 per cent of that amount was made up of taxes imposed upon the people of Canada. I am assuming for the purposes of argument that the House will agree that the customs tariff is a tax, and if you will agree to that, then 95 per cent of the whole amount
contributed to our treasury through the revenues of the country was made up of taxation. Now what do the figures show in these interesting accounts?
Let us take the last five years of this government's operations, and we find the average return from taxation to this government in the last five years to be $387,786,000. Was that great or was it not? We can judge only by comparing this statement with the figures in the five years preceding, under another government. You will find that the average taxation for the five years previous was $348,-
500,000.	So during the last five years this government has raised by taxation from the people of this country $39,280,000 more per year than was raised by its predecessors. Now what becomes of these wild statements of the Minister of Finance made annually in his budget speeches to the effect that ho has reduced the taxation by $24,000,000, $25,000,000 and $27,000,000, when the truth is, according to the public accounts laid before this House by his own department, he has taken well nigh $40,000,000 more per annum out of the pockets of the people by taxation than did his predecessors in the previous five years? What does that mean to the people of Canada? It is the burden of taxation that counts in regard to government financing; it is not the bulk amount of the tax, but the burden which that tax imposes upon the individual, that counts.
Now I take for the purposes of this illustration the statement made in this House by the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr Malcolm), in a very excellent speech whic! he delivered here last week, and for which he is to be complimented by the whole House of Commons. I take his statement of population for the year 1926, because he gets it from the officials of his own department. The population in that year was 9,390,000, and 1 find that the increased taxation during the last five years was $39,280,000 per annum Divide one by the other, and you find that for every man, woman and child in this country there has been a positive increase of taxation to the extent of $4.18 per annum For a family of five it would mean $20.90 per annum of increased taxation imposed by this government on the people of this coun try, over and above the taxation which was imposed for the five years before this government came into power. In making that statement I must make the further reservation, that five per cent of the amounts I have mentioned should come off, because S per cent does not represent taxation, but 9a per cent of the amounts which I have stated is derived from and represents actual taxation
The Budget-Mr. Guthrie

So that, instead of saying 34.18 per head, I should possibly say $3.98 per head. However the burden is enormous whichever way you take it, and these annual announcements of the Minister of Finance that he has greatly reduced the taxes of the people of this country are again purely imaginary. I object on the part of those who sit around me in this section of the House, to financial methods of this kind. We object that the financial statement laid before this House by the Finance minister in his budget speech was not a clear, fair and open presentation of the actual finances of the country. Where the minister's statement does not agree with the public accounts, we are bound to accept the statement contained in the public accounts, and I ask the Finance minister, before this debate closes, to explain to the House thpse very evident and serious discrepancies. We object to this budget because it has positively increased the burden of taxation on the people of the Dominion. These burdens should be lower, and they should have been lowered years ago. I have never yet heard a minister in this House, nor a Liberal speaker on a political platform in this Dominion, admit that the Liberal government itself has been the cause of much of the increased taxation. The other day a cheer went up in this chamber by government supporters when the minister announced a 20 per cent cut in the sales tax. Now it sounds as if he had done something substantial when he says, "I have reduced the sales tax by 20 per cent." The sales tax was five per cent, and he has taken one per cent from it, but for years he retained that sales tax upon the necessities of life at the rate of five per cent in spite of our protests. What Liberal speaker in parliament or out of parliament ever told the people that Liberal government had increased the sales tax? The Liberals placed that burdensome imposition on the people of Canada. When my hon. friend and his government took office in December, 1921, it is true we had the sales tax. It was a war measure imposed as a war tax, but it was only a tax of three per cent. At once upon taking office this government increased it to four and a half per cent; then they increased it to six per cent, despite our protests and objections. Then they found what we pointed out they would find, that they had actually created a hindrance to the commercial business of the country and they had to reduce it to five per cent. Now, with a great flourish of trumpets, the announcement, is made that the sales tax has been reduced to four per cent. That sale tax forms one of the heavy burdens upon the

common people of this country. It is one of the direct causes of the high cost of living in Canada. Does the government not realize that when the ordinary citizen of Canada goes out to buy a hundred dollars worth of the necessaries of life for himself, his wife and children, on every hundred dollars worth which he purchases-I do not mean foodstuffs but other necessaries-the treasury of Canada exacts five dollars from him or did so last year? This year it is going to exact from him four dollars on every hundred dollars' worth of purchases. In future when he buys a hundred dollars' worth of goods he can say to himself, "Well, I saved a dollar this time because this good Liberal government has taken one dollar tax off every hundred dollars' worth of purchases." He will now pay $4 of taxes instead of $5 upon every hundred dollars of purchases. That is the only relief the ordinary citizen of Canada has obtained through the budget. It has been called a rich man's budget, and so it is in every sense of the word.
I do not offer objection to the cut which has been made in the income tax. I say this reduction has been long delayed. This government has taken a long time to make up its mind to reduce taxation, but having decided to do something, it has certainly had regard for those who are best able to pay money into the treasury, and has had little regard for the ordinary man or woman, the ordinary citizen of Canada. To the ordinary citizen it hands back one dollar on every purchase of one hundred dollars' worth of the necessaries of life, while to the rich man it says again this year, as it said last year, "There is a plum for you in the budget reduction."
I had this matter figured out in the government department of taxation, and I find that in the case of the man with an income of $60,000 a year-and there are many in that class-the government has granted a reduction of $1107 on income tax, to the man with an income of $40,000 a year there is a reduction of $589; to the man enjoying an income of $20,000 a year, the government has granted relief to the extent of $154; to the man enjoying an income of $10,000 a year the reduction is $29, but to the great mass of the people of Canada the reduction is a single dollar on every purchase of a hundred dollars' worth of the necessaries of life.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
My recollection is that
it was, and there are some accumulation and arrears still to be collected, but the tax was taken off some years ago. However, it was a war tax when it was put on and was not intended to be permanent. The sales tax was similarly put on as a war burden and not intended to be permanent. It should at least have been cut in two this year and wiped out entirely next year. I can assure hon. members that the people of this country would have appreciated such a reduction although the rich men might possibly have had to wait a year or two longer for their relief. There is a tremendous number of people in this country who would have been cheered by the news that five dollars had been taken off every hundred dollars' worth of purchases of the necessaries of life which they might purchase from month to month throughout the year 1927. We object to the principle upon which this reduction of taxation has been arranged by the government. We do not think it is a proper one. We do not think the government has followed the principle of the greatest good to the greatest number. These reductions emphasize much more than any words of mine the fact that the present budget is in reality a rich man's budget and not a budget in the interests of the whole people of the Dominion.
Something has been said about the high cost of living; I think I said something myself at the beginning of my remarks on that subject. Is it not astounding, as pointed out by my hon. friend from West Calgary (Mr. Bennett), that the cost of living in this country in the month of December last, 1926, was higher than it has been since the year 1922 when this government came into power? The figures submitted to the House by the hon. member for West Calgary are not such as the government can quarrel with, for they are prepared by this government itself for the information of the House and the .people of Canada. The officials of this government have established that the cost of living to-day is almost at the peak since the year 1922. It costs the average family of five to-day, for the supply of the actual necessaries of life, $21.41 a week. If taxation has been reduced, if conditions have in any way been made easier,
why is the reduction not reflected in the cost of living in Canada? Why has the cost of living almost reached its maximum to-day? With a knowledge of the fact that the cost of living was about at its peak before the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) and before the Minister of Finance, why could not the minister have been sufficiently courageous to relieve the situation by abolishing the 5 per cent sales tax altogether and so give the ordinary people a chance?
Another thing to which we object is the fact that the budget gives no intimation whatever that the government is disposed in any way to economize in the management of the affairs of the country. This year in the main estimates the government proposes to spend $6,500,000 more than it did last year. We have not yet had the supplementary estimates, but no doubt [DOT] they will be very substantial. But, as I say, in the main estimates alone we have a proposed expenditure of six and a half millions more than we spent last year. What I have to say about the estimates is this. If the government had any real desire to economize they could take that blue volume of. estimates and, sitting around a table with the Minister of Finance and a blue pencil, they could go over the estimates page by page. If this were done it would be found that large items on every page could be blue pencilled. A vast sum of money could be saved this very year and no public service in the country would in any way be hindered or embarrassed.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: Militia?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
Yes, I have a word to
say about the militia. If there is one respect in which this government has been tardy- yes, careless-in the performance of its duties, if there is one respect in which it has absolutely failed, it is in the maintenance of a proper militia force in Canada. The most hopeful sign I have seen in regard to the present government in many a long day is the fact that to-day we have a gallant soldier (Mr. Ralston) at the head of the Department of National Defence, and his presence in the government must mean something, for we see a very substantial increase in the vote for national defence this year. We have been a long time waiting for this, and we are not here either to challenge or to criticise the increase, but to support the government in respect of it. But apart from that there are many other things in this blue book of estimates for 1927 that might still receive the attention of the government. Go over the
The Budget-Mr. Guthrie

harbours and rivers vote; go over the public buildings vote; take the estimates page by page, and you. can eliminate millions upon millions of dollars. If that were done the government would have some money to spend on some real development work in the Dominion.
I went over the estimates the other night, and I found what I have found in .them every year since this government took office. One thing they have never failed to do, is to increase the public service of Canada. There has never been a year that has not shown a substantial increase in the number of civil servants, with a correspondingly large increase in the amount of taxation thereby necessary. Save only three departments every department shows an increase of civil servants this year. I have them all tabulated, and I think there are only three departments that do not show an increase. The total number of new civil servants for whom salaries will have to be provided, if these estimates go through, will be 168, and the additional salary list amounts to $317,000, including, of course, statutory increases. But it has been so every year since this government assumed office. In regard to one thing, I think, we are all of one mind: the public service of Canada is overmanned. That being so, why further increase the number of civil servants? Those hon. members who were in the House when the late Frank McCrea was here must at that time have been convinced that the departments of the civil service were overmanned, not only the inside service but the outside service as well. Frank McCrea made it very clear. Why, therefore, increase the number? I am not asking the government to displace people who are now in the service, but there is no reason why the list should be increased every year by new appointments, when the government must know in its heart that the departments are overstaffed, as they have been for the last twenty-five years. Can we not call a halt in this matter? Can not a large sum of money be saved in this respect as well as in other respects in the present estimates?
In one respect the Minister of Finance has been fairly cautious in his predictions in regard to his financing during the current year 1927. This, I think, is the only occasion on which he has presented a budget when he has not given a fairly good forecast, based of course on estimate, of what would happen financially during the ensuing twelve months. For some reason only a very slight reference is made to such matters in the speech the minister delivered cm February 17, although he did say that he estimated that the revenues

for the next twelve months would be equal to those of the last twelve months, placing the revenue of the last twelve months at $393,006,000. But in announcing his reduction of taxation he had to point out that the figure just quoted would have to be reduced by $27,000,000, leaving him an estimated revenue of only $366,000,000 for the 'ensuing twelve months. Now the government has brought down estimates for $354,000,000 odd, besides railway estimates for $22,518,000 odd, making a total of some $376,000,000. Then we will have to deal with the supplementaries as well. I assume the supplementaries will be fairly substantial this year. Would I be right in placing them at $20,000,000, or is that too high? This year we expect that something will be done in the estimates for old age pensions, and we anticipate as well an inclusion in the supplementaries of a substantial sum to take care of maritime rights legislation. Is it therefore too much to say that the supplementaries will amount to $20,000,000? I do not think so. Well, if they do, then we have a program for expenditures in the next twelve months amounting to $396,000,000, while we have an estimated revenue of only $366,000,000.
In face of these facts the Minister of Finance comes to the House and declares that he expects to finance a good deal of the maturing obligations of the country next year out of ordinary revenue. The thing is impossible on the face of it. His estimates may be wrong, and I must say that they have been very vaguely placed on Hansard in the budget speech; this is the first time he has not given us a really concise statement as to the future financial operations of the government. What is next year's financing to be? On November 1 next, we have bonds maturing to the extent of over $29,000,000; these should be met. On November 15 next we have more maturing bonds amounting to about $S,000,000, which should be paid. Then again on December 1, we have further obligations maturing amounting to over $63,000,000 making in all, as the minister says, about $100,000,000. His statement in this House a few days ago of his expectations in regard to government financing this year, if it means anything at all, means that he will be met with a deficit flf from $20,000,000 to $30,000,000 on the program which has been laid before parliament, and will have nothing on hand out of which to pay maturing loans.
Is it not time, as suggested on this side of the House, for some settled policy to be adopted by this government in regard to the national debt of Canada? Some very con-

The Budget-Mr. Guthrie
structive suggestions have been made during this debate. The hon. member for West Calgary (Mr. Bennett) elaborated a plan which will require grave consideration and examination; he has offered a most constructive suggestion to this government, but will they do anything in regard to it? The hon. member for Toronto East Centre (Mr. Matthews) also brought this matter definitely to the attention of the government in a very carefully considered proposal; hon. members in other quarters of the House have made constructive suggestions also, but will the government act upon any of them or will they continue this go-as-you-please sort of financing in which they have indulged for the last five years? Will they continue this happy-go-lucky policy in regard to these maturing obligations, or will they themselves suggest some definite scheme, either by the annual appropriation of a fixed amount, or by some manner of conversion, or by some device of a sinking fund, or by some other definite plan, whereby we may take care of the enormous national debt of Canada as it matures and whereby this debt may not be spread over too many future generations? Why, Sir, if this government had shown the least anxiety; if within the past three years it had displayed a little business sagacity and had prevented that raid upon the treasury which robbed us of anywhere from $50,000,000 to $100,000,000 as disclosed in the customs and excise scandal, we might have had something substantial with which to discharge our obligations. We could probably have taken care of the whole one hundred million dollars maturing this year. These are some of the reasons why we who sit to your left, Sir, are opposed to this budget, but there are other matters, and if I do not weary the House too much I would like to dwell upon some of these.
We object that during its whole career the Liberal government has failed to initiate or suggest any real progressive policy for the development of Canada. For nearly six years this government has simply rested upon its oars; it has closed its ears to the appeals of our citizens east, west and centre, and we stand to-day after six years of rule by this Liberal government so far as the development of Canada is concerned practically where we started. Does the government realize that for four or five years at least appeals have been made year by year and almost month by month by the people of the three maritime provinces, asking for the redress of their grievances and for the righting of the injustices under which they are suffering? Does this government realize that year after year
it has turned a deaf ear to these appeals? Never a hand turned, and never an action of any kind until on the eve of a general election, Sir Andrew Duncan was called upon to make an investigation. Why did not the government act of its own motion in these intervening years? Simply because of its supineness, its lack of initiative, its incapacity to deal with the big problems which confront this Dominion. This lack of initiative has had just as baneful an effect in western Canada as in eastern Canada. Why, Sir, let me refer to a famous speech made by the leader of the government in the constituency of North York in September, 1925, when he acknowledged to the electors that the country was practically stagnating. He said, "I cannot go on any longer in this way; I am not able to deal with the great problems which confront the government of this country." He made that confession to the people of Canada, and said, "This is the time to march forward." The people have given him a new lease of power and have placed him firmly in control of the government of this country, and the people will expect from now on that he and this government will do something substantial towards the development of Canada.
We hear criticism from the west in regard to railway rates. I listened very attentively to a very able speech on that subject delivered last night by the hon. member for Saskatoon (Mr. Young). The situation in western Canada with regard to railway rates is a disgrace to this country, and has been for some time past. Cannot the government suggest a remedy for the existing situation in that regard? Parliament declared in June 1925 that a certain line of action should be taken in regard to railway rates, but nothing has been concluded in the interval. The whole of northern Saskatchewan and northern Alberta are suffering from an unjust discrimination in connection with grain rates. Until yesterday my impression was that this discrimination had been removed a month or two ago, but I learned from the speech of the hon. member for Saskatoon last night that discrimination still exists. What is the government going to do? We have a Board of Railway Commissioners; are they not capable of dealing with this problem? I make no reflection upon the members of the board; they are human and one man can only do the work of one man. The applications which have come 'before the board are applications requiring very grave consideration; they have great ramifications, but if we have not enough railway commissioners to promptly deal with these important questions, let us change the system; either let us have more commissioners
The Budget-Mr. Guthrie

or let us make two boards out of the commissioners we now have. I never could understand why it was necessary to have six commissioners dealing with one case. In the province of Ontario we suffered in the same way in the appellate division of the Supreme court, and there we simply divided the judges into two courts, which removed the difficulty at once. Could this not be done in regard to the railway board? It is a scandal that in this country a great question like that of the freight rates of western Canada should be held up for a year and a half-yes, well on to two years-that it is still under consideration, still under argument, and the people of northern Alberta, northern Saskatchewan and northern Manitoba still overcharged two cents per hundred in respect of their grain shipments. Can the government do nothing with respect to that Situation? We can bring it to their attention, we can force it to their notice, but we as an opposition have no power to move in the matter. I said that the government have little of initiation about them. I am afraid it is too true. I have suggested a solution; will the government even examine my suggestion, or will they be content simply to twirl their thumbs, to pursue their happy-go-lucky course-the course they have pursued up to now-dreaming away their time, neglecting their opportunities, enjoying the sweets and emoluments of office, and allowing the people of the three prairie provinces -at least in the northern sections-to pay two cents a hundred extra on the grain that goes out of that country? This is a sleepy government. I suggest a motto for this government; it occurs to me now. I do not suppose any members of the government will recognize this motto save my hon. friend the Minister of Immigration (Mr. Forke) as it occurs in the Book of Proverbs. The motto of this government should be:
Yet a little sleep, a little slumber, a little folding of the hands to sleep.
If we can, we are going to awaken the government with respect to various questions. One question is the freight rates question. Another question is the development of the new territory in that western country. To most of us it is a revelation to know that we have still a perfect western empire ready for settlement. All we require is railway facilities and people to settle that country. I regret to say that I feel humiliated when I come to the question of settlement in western Canada. I believe the government will feel humiliated also. I do not blame, I cannot blame, the present Minister of Im-

migration for the sad condition that now exists. He is not responsible for it, nor can the staff of the Immigration department be blamed; it is a well-run department, well staffed with capable men. But I blame the government. The whole policy of the government with regard to immigration has been a policy of exclusion. There is nothing we want in Canada so much as people, and the government has done nothing so definitely as excluding people from Canada.
What, Mr. Speaker, is the result of the efforts of this government in regard to immigration in the three prairie provinces? It is a sad commentary on the efforts of this government to settle these great provinces. We know that a census is taken in the three prairie provinces every five years. One was taken in June, of last year. What does it disclose? It discloses that the five year effort of the Liberal government to bring settlers to the province of Manitoba has resulted in an increase of population in the province of 28,938, or a four and a half per cent increase in five years. We know that the natural increase is one per cent per annum. That increase is obtained by reason of the fact that there are more births than deaths. In five years we should have had an increase in population in Manitoba of about 32,000 people, the natural increase without a single immigrant coming into that province. We have an increase shown by the census returns of only 28,938 all told. What has become of our natural increase? What has become of the eighty or ninety thousand people which this government has brought into that country annually? At the opening of this session I said that I thought there was a considerable exodus from western Canada to the United States, but I was checked up by the Minister of Immigration who said such people were only going away to spend the winter in California or the like.

speechtext: I said they might be going there.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
I think on hearing these figures my hon. friend will revise that statement. What have the former increases been in Manitoba? In 1906, the population of Manitoba was 365,000. In 1911, it had risen to 461,000, an increase in five years of 94,000 From 1911 to 1916 it rose to 553,000, an increase in the five year period of 92,000. From 1916 to 1921-war years too-it rose to 610,000, an increase of 57,000; and from 1921 down to 1926, the increase was 28,938 souls, some three or four thousand less than the natural increase

The Budget-Mr. Guthrie
should have shown. I am sorry to say that the figures disclose something else. Four of the constituencies in that province have actually lost population. I do not know that I had better name them; anybody who gets this return from the Bureau of Statistics, the preliminary report of the census of Manitoba for 1926, can find these things out for himself. Take the province of Saskatchewan, a great province offering such fine opportunities for settlement. The increase during five years was 63,532, or nine per cent. They evidently retained their natural increase and got four per cent more. But listen to the figures: In 1906, Saskatchewan had 257,000 people; by 1911 the population had jumped to 492,000, an increase in five years of 235.000. From 1911 to 1916, under the Conservative regime, the population jumped to 647,000, an increase of 155,000 in five years. Under the Liberal government during the last five years the population has increased from 757,000 to 821,000, a paltry increase of 63,000 or nine per cent. And some of the constituencies in Saskatchewan have actually been reduced in population since the census of 1921.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: I do not want to interrupt, but my hon. friend will remember that during that period the great question of re-establishing the returned men was dealt with, and those figures were included.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: That ought to make the population greater.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: I thought my hon. friend was counting the returned soldiers as immigrants.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
I am not talking of immigrants, I am talking of the total population. The point I am seeking to make is that the population is not by any means what it should be.
Now, take the province of Alberta. In 1906, that province had a population of 185,000. By 1911 it had jumped by 179,000 and reached 374,000. Then under the Conservative government from 1911 to 1916 it jumped again to 496,000, an increase in five years of 122,000. From 1916 to 1921, even in the war years, it jumped again by 92,000. For the last five years, under the present government, it has gone from 588,000 to 607,000, an increase of only 19,000 in the population in the great province of Alberta in five years. That is an increase of just 3^ per cent, or 1J per cent less than the natural increase in that province. Where, we ask, have the people gone? We hope they have come to eastern Canada or gone to British Columbia. Certainly they are not to be found in the prairie provinces. The statement issued by the government itself through the Dominion Bureau of Statistics is a sad commentary on the efforts of this Liberal government to develop western Canada in the way of bringing in new population.
Before concluding my remarks I desire to touch on only one or two other matters. This House was pleased the other evening to hear a new declaration of policy uttered by the Minister of Railways (Mr. Dunning) on behalf of the government. It was not an utterance made upon the spur of the moment; it was a carefully considered statement in writing said to have been prepared by the Minister of Finance himself and handed to the Minister of Railways for delivery to the House of Commons. We on this side noticed that my hon. friend was somewhat nervous during the delivery of that statement to the House. He seemed to be out of place, to be very nervous. At times he seemed almost to choke over it. Perhaps he found that he had some hard swallowing; but nevertheless he got through it, and now we have reason to know, if we can place any dependence upon the formal pronouncements of this government that we have in power, a government favourable to the policy of protection, favourable to the policy which since 1879 has been the established fiscal policy of the Dominion of Canada, notwithstanding the efforts of this present Liberal administration during the last five years to render that policy useless and innocuous by continually tinkering and tampering with it. We take some satisfaction from the statement that has been delivered by the Minister of Railways upon behalf of the government, upon that subject
There never has been a moment's doubt as to the position of the Conservative party upon the question of protection. We look upon it as one of the corner stones in the foundation of our national structure. We believe that when the policy of protection was established in 1879 by the great Conservative leader of that time, it actually saved this country from bankruptcy, and from that day down to the advent of the present government in 1922 the policy of protection has remained practically intact in this country as the guiding principle of fiscal policy under every government. I have heard many a Liberal speak of the prosperity of Canada under the Laurier-Fielding regime. I have heard many a Liberal speak of the Laurier-Fielding tariff and praise it to the skies. I was one of its supporters. In its day it was a good tariff; and it was the tariff of the Conservative party inaugurated by Sir John A. Macdonald in 1879, and the moment the
The Budget-Mr. Guthrie

present Prime Minister of Canada, the head of this government, undertook to interfere with the principle of protection in the customs tariff his interference was immediately reflected most adversely in the trade and industry of this Dominion.
It is some relief to know that further assaults on the system of protection will not be made in the future. It is some relief to know from the lips of the Minister of Finance and his colleague, the Minister of Railways, that they too believe in the stability of the customs tariff founded upon protective principles. This principle is now and will continue to be an outstanding plank in the policy of the Conservative party. There is no mistaking that statement. We do not advocate the policy of high protection which is attributed to us by ministers in this government. We are not high protectionists; we do not seek "higher and higher and higher protection." Nobody in the Conservative party seeks or desires any such thing-nobody suggests it. We ask for reasonable, adequate protection, protection that will protect, protection that will give fair and equal advantage and opportunity to every class and condition in this country, bearing equally and fairly upon all and harshly upon none.

If the hon. member were
returned to power, would he increase the present tariff?
