I cannot answer that
question without first making a full examination of the whole situation.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: Oh, oh.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
Anything like an examination of a situation or a considered judgment upon an intricate question always raises a laugh on the other side. I am sorry to say that this government is lacking in many respects. In the first place, it lacks in examination and consideration; in the second place, it lacks in initiation, .and in the third place, it lacks courage. During one of the hectic days of last session, one of those occasions when the Minister of Finance thought his government was in danger, although it actually pulled through, he said while shaking his fist at that corner of the House: You know what it means if you defeat this government; it means "protection and higher and higher and higher protection." I know the Minister of Railways deals in

language of that kind, both in the House and on the platform out west, and I know moreover he uses it simply as a bogey to frighten and to threaten the people of those western provinces. He uses it as the nurse did to the children in the old nursery rhyme, Which says:
The goblins will get you if you don't watch out.
I believe enlightenment will come to those provinces in the near future as to the real attitude of the Conservative party, upon the question of protection. I believe the time will come when they will appreciate and endorse our attitude. We are not selfish in regard to the policy of protection. We do not ask for any "brick for brick" tariff. We do not ask for higher and higher protection as attributed to us by our opponents. We ask merely for a reasonable, adequate tariff measure, and if we get it, we believe it will redound to the advantage of every class and of every part of the Dominion.
I can appreciate just as clearly as can the Minister of Railways that with an agricultural community such as we have in the western provinces, who produce mostly grain and cattle, it is difficult, if not impossible, to confer any direct benefit by a customs tariff. I realize that; it needs no demonstration; but I realize just as fully that it is absolutely necessary to the life of industry in eastern Canada that protection be maintained. Under such circumstances is it beyond the realm of statesmanship to equalize conditions in a country such as this? We have to recognize either now or some day in the future that we have a long straggling country, of great length and narrow breadth. We have many different interests and different communities. Our activities in life are greatly diversified, and some day we shall have to meet upon common ground in order that equal benefit and advantage shall be conferred by this Dominion of Canada upon all sections and classes of the people. The proposal of the Right Hon. Arthur Meighen last fall, when he was leader of the Conservative party met the situation better than any other proposal I have heard. He proposed to meet it on the basis of preferential freight rates.
One thing we must realize is the question of transportation costs in Canada. We cannot settle that question upon the basis of a single rate for all parts of Canada. Such a plan will not work out; it will disrupt this country. We have to recognize the special claims of the maritimes, so well pointed out by Sir Andrew Duncan, in respect of railway

The Budget-Mr. Guthrie
rates, and we on this side of the House are prepared to meet that recommendation.
But we shall have to apply the very same reasoning to the people in other sections of Canada. The raising of grain, the raising of those wonderful crops in the three prairie provinces, is a matter of the greatest interest to the people of Canada; it is a matter of interest to our trade and commerce, it is a matter of great national concern and if the present railway rates bear too heavily upon those basic commodities, then it is in the national interest that relief be given. Such in brief was the doctrine enunciated by the Right Hon. Arthur Meighen, and I am sorry to say that the west did not respond to his proposal. We shall have to come to it in the near future. Will the government initiate some policy of that kind? Is it utterly devoid of any power of initiation? Does it not realize that the question of preferential freight rates has to be settled? We in this country must learn to offset geographical conditions in the matter of freight charges. Already in our railway tariff mileage is disregarded, and we shall likewise have to disregard geography. We have done so in many cases already. We have given special rates over our railways to special industries to enable them to market their goods profitably, and so we shall have to do in regard to the grain and cattle growers of the west, and the time to do it is now, not to wait. We invite the government to make suggestions, and to propound a policy in regard to this great question. Grain and cattle being the staple productions of those three prairie provinces, and being vitally essential to the success and prosperity of the Dominion of Canada, can we not afford to give a preferential rate on the transportation of these products in the general interest of Canada. And I say the same with regard to coal, fish lumber and the like, from the maritime provinces. Already we have established a preferential rate in regard to certain products of British Columbia. Salmon has a preferential rate. Apples from the Okanagan come to the city of Montreal almost as cheaply as apples from the city of Toronto, because of the preferential rate they enjoy. Pulp and newsprint have preferential rates. Why not adopt that principle in regard to grain and in regard to live stock in the west, in regard practically to all the basic productions of this country, which by reason of geographical conditions are now too remote for profitable marketing? That brings me to another point.
It is an odd thing to me that from the city of Calgary to the city of Vancouver, which is so near at hand, only 642 miles distant, the farmers should be called upon to pay a

rate of 21 cents for transporting their grain, while all they are charged if they ship it to Fort William is 26 cents. The distance from Calgary to Fort William is 1,251 miles, and the rate is 26 cents; the distance from Calgary to Vancouver is 642 miles, and the rate is 21 cents. Why cannot that rate be placed upon a fair basis in order to give the farmers who ship from Calgary or Edmonton the advantage which should be theirs by reason of their proximity to Vancouver? Why impose upon them a higher rate than is imposed upon the traffic that goes eastward? For my part, I cannot see any reason in it. That is another matter which this government will have to settle, and it should be settled when the question of preferential rates is being settled in this country. I am satisfied it will have to be done at some time in the near future.
Then look at the coal problem, so dependent upon that very question. The coal problem has been pressed upon this government for the last five years, session after session, time and time again. The Minister of the Interior (Mr. Stewart) who is in charge of the coal matter is not at present in his seat. It Was said of him in this House by my hon. friend from Fort William (Mr. Manion) the other night that no man could be as honest as the Minister of the Interior looked. I say that no minister should be as dilatory as the Minister of the Interior has been for the last five years in regard to this coal problem. Now he seems to take the ground that the matter cannot be settled at all, that it is economically impossible. Why, Mr. Speaker, if our coal supply was cut off to-morrow by the authorities of the United States, we would settle the coal question in Canada in twenty-four hours. But again, this government lacks initiative. Again, it lacks resolution. Again, it lacks courage. It has failed in every development scheme that it has undertaken. The Peace river scheme is as dead now almost as Julius Caesar. The settlement of the railway rate question has not been advanced since 1925. Immigration and settlement in the west has been a complete failure during the last five years. The question of transporting Alberta and Nova Scotia coal .to central Canada is just where it was five years ago, except for the effort of the Honourable Howard Ferguson, Conservative Premier of Ontario. These great questions all await a solution, and yet all my hon. friend, the Minister of Finance, says in his budget speech in regard to them, is: We must have faith. I will refer him to the Second Epistle of James, to look up a text for him-
The Budget-Mr. Guthrie

self: "But wilt thou know, 0 vain man, that faith without works is dead?" This government protests that it has faith, but it does nothing to justify that faith. It has been deplorably lacking in works. We have had no progressive action in the past and we want action in Canada in all these respects. Your financial program has resulted in nothing. Your efforts to reduce taxation have resulted in increasing it. Your efforts to reduce the cost of living have brought the cost of living to the highest peak to-day that we have reached since 1922. Your theory that tinkering and tampering with the tariff would reduce prices is the purest kind of fallacy. Just apply a test now and see what has been accomplished in regard to prices under your tariff tinkering propensities.
It has been argued in this House that if you reduce the tariff, you decrease the price to the consumer. A greater fallacy was never uttered. Let me premise my remarks with this statement: The government did not touch the customs tariff on furniture, and the price of furniture in the last six years has been reduced from 25 to 30 per cent. How? The reduction in price has been brought about by internal competition among furniture manufacturers. You allowed the furniture men reasonable protection, and competition among themselves has reduced the price from 25 to 30 per cent below the price of six years ago.
This government did not alter the customs tariff on boots and shoes, and the price of boots and shoes to-day is 40 per cent lower than it was six years ago. Internal competition, again, has reduced the price.
You did tamper with the woollen schedule, and with baneful results. The duty was 30 per cent net on woollens when you took power and you reduced it to 27J and subsequently cut off another 10 per cent more on the British preference. What happened to the woollens? There was little or no reduction in price. In some cases there was an increase in the price of woollen goods in Canada over six years ago. You took the duty off fertilizers, I think 10 per cent, and the price of fertilizers has been increased appreciably since. Twenty years ago you experimented and took the duty off binder twine and it has been doubled in price ever since.	*
But the outstanding feature in tariff tinker-ng is your operation in regard to agricultural mplements. That was a major operation on he part of the King government when it took rower in this country. Agricultural implements had a modest protective duty. The duty on binders was 12i per cent, and it was cut down to six per cent by this government. All

kinds of special privileges were granted to manufacturers of agricultural implements in regard to free material. Sales taxes were taken off and the like, and the government proclaimed to the farmers of this country that, a reduction in price would follow. The cut was wiped out and every advantage was given them. What was the result? I am speaking according to the book. Take binders and mowers. First I will give the prices of McCormick, Deering and International binders and then I will give the Massey-Harris prices afterwards. A six-foot binder with carrier in the year 1921, the last year of the Meighen government, sold at S235. In 1927, effective now, the price for the same six-foot binder with carrier is $239.
Any improvement?

None, none of a major
character. I have this from a reliable authority; the tariff was taken off and free materials given them. The sales tax of five per cent was taken off, and a binder to-day is just four dollars higher than in 1921. Then take a six-foot binder with carrier and a tongue truck. These are the net cash prices. In December 1921 the price was $252. The price to-day is $254, and the country is out the revenue and the workmen have had to leave Canada. The price of a seven-foot binder with carrier and tongue truck in December 1921 was $258, and the price to-day is $260. The price of an eight-foot binder with carrier and tongue truck in December 1921 was $266, and to-day it is $268.50.
Let us try Massey-Harris prices and see how they agree.
What point does my hon. friend take when he gives the prices?

These prices were all
based on Ontario. In the case of Winnipeg it would be the same price but the freight would have to be added.
The retail price?

I am quoting from the
retail price lists.
At the factory?

I do not know whether it is at the factory or at the station, but I am giving enough information to let the House know that prices have not been decreased but have been increased. I have not the 1921 prices for the Massey-Harris, but the 1919 prices. The 1919 price of No. 5 seven-foot binder, three-horse, was $233, truck, $9, sheaf-

The Budget-Mr. Guthrie
carrier, $8, total $250. The cash price to-day of a seven-foot three-horse binder is $260, truck $11, sheaf-carrier $9, total price 8280. The difference between the 1919 price and the price to-day is $30, and in the interval the tariff has been reduced and sales tax cut off, and the market thrown open for the free importation of raw materials. The farmers of Canada are paying an increased price for binders to-day and the treasury has lost all the revenue. Now I go a step further.
Would my hon. friend be good enough to give the House the cost of binders and mowers and that class of goods immediately prior to the last reduction of taxation?

Tell me the year you
want.

Immediately
prior to the last reduction of taxation.
Tell me the year you want and I will give you the price.

I want the
years 1923 and 1924.
I have the years 1923 and 1924, but not in my hand. I will get them.

Will you be
good enough to let us have them?

What has been the effect of that reduction in duty upon the trade of Canada, the industry of Canada, and the employment in Canada? Why some of us were shocked in the years 1918 and 1919 to know that the importation of agricultural implements into this country was between three and a half and four million dollars. We believed then, and believe now, that practically all of these goods could have been made just as well by Canadian workmen in .Canadian factories, but when the customs tariff on agricultural implements was reduced by the King government when it came into power our friends in the republic to the south of us were not slow to take advantage of the situation. The trade figures received yesterday from the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Malcolm) are very illuminating on that point. They show the importation of agricultural implements for the years ending January 31st, 1925, 1926 and 1927. In the year 1925, which would be the first full year under the operation of the cut in the tariff, the imports of agricultural implements rose to $6,367,877. In 1926 that figure had risen to $11,632,231, and during the last twelve months it has risen to $17,731,516, almost all
of which goods could have been made in this country, and a large percentage of which are now being made at Buffalo and Chicago by Canadian workmen who formerly had employment in Canada. That is a serious matter for the industry of this Dominion. It is a serious loss in implements and wages, and it is a serious loss to the treasury of Canada. We have lost the revenue which would have been received under the higher rate of duty and from sales tax but that perhaps is the least of our losses. All of this time our farmers have been dreaming away in a sort of charmed slumber, imagining they were getting cheaper implements. They have been deceived by the idea throughout eastern Canada and western Canada that the reduction in the tariff on agricultural implements was actually giving them cheaper implements. They will awaken from that slumber some day, and realize the real situation. The day will come when this protection bogey cannot be paraded by the Minister of Railways in the west against the Conservative party. I hope that when the hon. minister goes west next time he will tell the people the actual situation, and I hope he will tell the people of the western provinces that the Conservative party is not a high protectionist party.
I certainly will not.

Well, then, if I am for the time being the leader of this party, I state it on my responsibility as leader that high protection is not the policy of the Conservative party of Canada. Although I have no doubt the Minister of Railways (Mr. Dunning) will stick to his statement that he will not so admit. However, that is only one of the planks of our platform.
I read the other day, or someone told me, that about seventy or eighty years ago Benjamin Disraeli, at that time leader of the Tory party in England-I use the word "Tory" out of deference to the Minister of Railways, and because we are proud of the name-had but one motto, namely, that the Tory party would always resist revolution and assist progress- one of those neat, epigrammatic statements for which the late Benjamin Disraeli was famous. And, Mr. Speaker, the Tory party in Canada is a party that will always resist revolution. We stand, Sir, for the maintenance of law and order in every corner of the Dominion; and we stand also to assist any progressive movement even though a Liberal government may initiate it. Anything which contributes to the progress and development of eastern or western or central Canada will have our full support. I do not mean, of course,
The Budget-Mr. Guthrie

that we are prepared to support everything without examination or consideration, as my hon. friends over there would seek to have us do. We will examine and investigate, but every meritorious proposal for the development or the advancement of the country, whether in the west, in the east or in the' central part of the country, will have our support. That is a leading principle of this party.
This party has a record for progressive legislation second to none. It is a party whose record goes back to confederation year and beyond it; a party which was the first to establish and maintain the fiscal policy of this country upon a sound basis, under which policy Canada has made great measure of progress; a party Which first started settlement and development in the west; a party which aided the construction of the first transportation line, in spite of opposition from every quarter of the Liberal ranks; a party which in the dark days of railroading in Canada had in the Right Hon. Arthur Meighen a leader bold enough, courageous enough, confident enough to grapple with that mighty problem which was bequeathed as a legacy from a former Liberal administration-a man who took hold of scattered lines of railway in Canada which were on the point of bankruptcy, some of Which indeed were actually bankrupt, and who so arranged matters that we have to-day evolved a great national transcontinental railway system under the ownership of the people of Canada. These are steps in the record of the Conservative party so far as the progress and development of the country are concerned. And we propose to go ahead. We propose to insist that this government shall do likewise and that there shall be no lagging behind in the next few years during which the government may be in office. The last five or six years, so far as any real progress has been concerned, have been nothing short of a disgrace to any government. Hon. gentlemen opposite have done nothing; they have got nowhere. The country to all intents and purposes is just where it was six years ago. We intend to see to it that in the future there shall be no more standing idle, but that the march forward, heralded by the Prime Minister (Mr! Mackenzie King) at Richmond Hill in 1925, shall now begin. The command to march is going to be given and the trumpets are going to sound, and we shall insist on going forward. And if the government goes forward on reasonable, logical and progressive grounds it will have our assistance at every step.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. A. ROBB (Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The budget delivered on February 17 was so well received in this House and throughout the country, by the press friendly to the government as well as by the opposing press, that I had made up my mind not to offer any further observations upon the motion and the amendment thereto, and this not out of any disrespect to my hon. friend from Macleod (Mr. Coote) who presented the amendment, but simply because I felt that hon. members were anxious to get on with the business of the House and also because I knew that every Monday and Wednesday occupied in debating the budget were so many days lost to private members who had certain resolutions which they desired to have discussed. Not until yesterday did I come to the conclusion that I should add a word or two to what I have already said on the motion now before the House; and I wish to assure hon. gentlemen who are anxious to speak before the debate close's that I shall take up but a very few moments of their time.
The official leader of the opposition (Mr. Guthrie) has this afternoon maintained his reputation for eloquence as well as for adroitly skating round the question. I have been associated in public life with my hon. friend for many years. Listening to him this afternoon, I could recall one day down in the old museum where he and I conspired to make some trouble for the then government, and he was, if anything, more eloquent then than he was to-day. The hon. gentleman has said that the debate has been worth while inasmuch as it has brought out some new ideas. With that I agree. Indeed, early in his speech, I had made some notes of points on which I felt inclined to agree with him; I was prepared to agree with him on most of the questions he was discussing, apart from the balance sheet. But as he proceeded to his peroration it occurred to me that my hon. friend should this afternoon be clothed in sackcloth and ashes and should be weeping for his own attacks on that great Conservative party which he has been so loudly praising; because in former days we had no more violent champion in the Liberal ranks than my good friend the official leader of the opposition. I remember how sound he was in 1911 when we appealed to the country on the question of larger and wider markets for western Canada.
I shall not enter into any lengthy discussion of the remarks of the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens) and the leader of the opposition regarding the balance

The Budget-Mr. Robb
sheet. The budget as presented to the House calls for no defence. In 1924, as I remember, I was subject to attacks of the same nature as those that have been made in this debate, and they did not come from that side of the House either, but from gentlemen on this side who, the following year or two years afterwards, admitted that I had been right. I fancy that when the public accounts come down a year from now my hon. friend from Vancouver Centre and the leader of the opposition will have to admit that on this occasion too I have been in the right. After listening to the speech of my hon. friend from Vancouver Centre I sent word to the department inquiring how it was that Mr. Stevens had arrived at the figures he had presented to the House. The reply came back, "The member for Vancouver Centre has made the mistake of adding together your estimated surpluses with an actual reduction." That would be all right to an ordinary layman like myself, but not to a well posted chartered accountant, so I will have to ask my hon. friend to come down and talk it over with the Auditor General.

Of course that is not
what he did.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Both my hon. friends have
also, I believe quite sincerely, overlooked in their calculations the fact that in 1922 we had $144,000,000 of temporary loans which since then have either been paid off or entered in the funded debt.
With the observations of the last speaker in regard to the reduction of expenditure in carrying on the affairs of the country I am quite prepared to agree. The Minister of Finance is never in favour of additional expenditures, but my hon. friend has had experience as a member of a government, and indeed showed this afternoon that in one particular department with which he was once associated, he was not very much in favour of economy. That is the experience of the Minister of Finance; every day for weeks before the presentation of the budget deputations from all parts of Canada come to see him; they come from as far east as Halifax and Prince Edward Island and from as far west as Vancouver. These deputations are about evenly divided between those who desire increased expenditure and those who want economy or a reduction in taxation, and in that way it is rather hard to balance your budget. My hon. friend the leader of the opposition in criticizing our expenditure was very careful not to say what particular expenditure he would reduce. I submit it to the judgment of every hon. member of this House who took part in the 'last campaign, that while my hon. friends were always in favour of economy they wanted that economy practised in the other fellow's country. Will any person say that the official leader of the great Conservative party in the last campaign was opposed to the construction of the Hudson Bay railway, or that his party opposed the continued deepening of the Welland canal? Those are the two large expenditures which enter into our increase in the estimates as presented.
Before I proceed, Mr. Speaker, if I may be allowed a personal word I would like to thank all hon. members of this House, my hon. friends opposite and hon. gentlemen in the far corner as well as those who sit behind me, for the altogether too kind words used towards myself. I desire particularly to thank my friend who immediately preceded me, speaking as official critic of the opposition.
My friend the former Minister of Finance (Mr. Bennett) tried to represent to the country that our reductions in taxation were pure myths, that they only existed in the imagination of the Minister of Finance, and he submitted a well thought out and carefully prepared statement of percentages to show that the taxes were actually greater than they had been prior to the reductions; he built up a story to show that these reductions, so stated, were but will-o'-the-wisps, to lead the people along. But, Mr. Speaker, the reductions presented to this House in the budget for the year 1926, when a long list of reductions in the income tax was introduced, were not myths to those who had to pay. The man who was called upon to pay $100 in 1925 but who discovered the day after the budget was presented that he only had to pay $30 did not consider it a myth; he had enough money left to buy an additional suit of clothes for himself or for some member of his family. The man with a revenue of $3,000, who formerly had to pay $40 but who in 1926 did not have to pay one cent, did not consider these reductions a myth. The reductions in taxation presented last year gave a wide measure of relief to a large section of Canada. Hon. gentlemen have complained that in some cases the income tax was increased, and I admit frankly to-day as I did last year that in preparing these revisions in the income tax the policy was to make it easier for people with earned incomes rather than for those with unearned
The Budget-Mr. Robb

incomes, and I admit that the latter class have to pay a little more. I will deal with that in a moment, however.
My hon. friend said that the reductions in the sales tax did not amount to anything, and he submitted a list of percentages to show that there was an increase this year as compared with last year. No person knows better than does the ex-Minister of Finance that the reductions in the sales tax were very real. As a matter of fact the reductions in that tax this year are not the only reductions which have been made by this government since it assumed office. In 1924 we made sweeping reductions in the sales tax, exempting altogether most of the agricultural machinery and the implements required for the other basic industries of mining, lumbering and fisheries. At that time hon. gentlemen opposite opposed those reductions, which in that year amounted to $24,725,000, in round figures. In 1925 we made further reductions in the sales tax amount ing to $400,000 and in 1926 we again reduced that tax either by exempting certain articles altogether or by reductions which brought about a loss of $300,000, while this year it is estimated that the reduction will amount to about $16,000,000. Altogether since this government has been entrusted with the responsibilities of office we have made reductions in the sales tax totalling over $41,000,000.
My friend the leader of the opposition (Mr. Guthrie) said, "Yes, it is very true that you have made certain reductions in the sales tax but you increased the sales tax," and he quotes certain figures to show that that sales tax at a certain period of 1922 was 2J per cent, and that we had increased it to 6 per cent. What are the facts? In 1923 that tax was increased by Mr. Fielding to a maximum of 6 per cent. The average under the old tax enacted by my friends the Conservatives when Sir Henry Drayton was Minister of Finance was 2J per cent. But that tax was capable of pyramiding; in many cases, notably boots and shoes, it was pyramided until the actual tax was 8i per cent. Boots and shoes were taxed from the hide right through the leather and from the wholesaler to the retailer, and instead of that tax amounting to 2 per cent, as is the case this year, it was 8i per cent under the administration of my friends opposite.
The same statement would apply to clothing; the leader of the opposition found some fault with me because I did not altogether wipe out the sales tax on clothing. That is not original with my hon. friend; we had delegations coming to the office representing different industries, among them gentlemen who said they represented the clothing indus-

try, but at the same time we had letters warning us to be careful of these representatives, who were urging that we altogether remove the sales tax from clothing. Now I had an experience of that in 1924, when I reduced the sales tax on boots and shoes from six per cent to three per cent. And what was that experience? There are widely scattered throughout this country, for instance, many clothing merdhants with small capital. At the present they buy a stock; they pay the sales tax. But the next day the Minister of Finance presents his budget, and he wipes out the five per cent sales tax. Well, when that is done it takes away five per cent of that merchant's capital. That is a hardship upon him, and I say frankly to my hon. friends opposite -as I said to this delegation, and they agreed with me-that the proper method of reducing this sales tax-and I agree with my hon. friends that as fast as possible the sales tax should be taken off-is to take it off gradually so that it will do no harm to anyone.
I said a moment ago that I was not going to follow my hon. friend in his attack on the balance sheet as presented, but one conclusive proof that this government has reduced the funded public debt of this country and reduced also the charges which the people are compelled to pay for carrying that funded debt, is the fact that the interest charges upon that funded debt have been considerably reduced. If a man with a mortgage on his farm pays $100 in interest this year and only has to pay $80 next year, he knows that the mortgage has been reduced to that extent.
Or the interest rate.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
But the reduction in the interest does not account for all the reductions that I would show here. In 1921-22 the total interest charges amounted to over $135,000,000. In 1922-23 the interest charges amounted to $137,000,000. My hon. friend made a reference to the public accounts. Well hon. gentlemen opposite can refer to the volume for themselves and on page 46 they will find additions that were made to the public debt during their administration. What was the total interest on the public funded debt last year? It amounted to $124,000,000, as compared with $137,000,000 in 1922-23. That, Sir, is the answer I give to my hon. friend.
Now let me deal briefly with the amendment of my hon. friend from Macleod (Mr. Coote). I can quite understand the necessity of keeping a party together by proposing an amendment that they can all get together on and vote for, but I think my hon. friend will find himself in rather an embarrassing position

The Budget-Mr. Robb
when he goes back to his electors, because I wonder if he will not find on the platform opposed to him-none of us are elected by acclamation; I have never had that experience and I imagine my hon. friend will be no better off-some person who will get up on the platform and quote Hansard to show where this hon. gentleman asked me to do some of the very things that I am doing today, that is, making reductions in the taxation. Now my hon. friend in his attempt to defeat the government-because the motion if carried can have no other effect-will be accused of putting into power a gentleman who this afternoon made a speech indicating that if he and his friends got into office the tariff on some articles in this country will be so high-as said by one of their supporters in my hearing in the last election-that the sun could not shine over it on St. James street, Montreal, until half past eleven in the morning.
I am sure the minister will agree that is not what the leader of the opposition said this aftemoi

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I admit that my hon. friend the official leader of the oppi sition, speaking this afternoon, made, with his customary ability, a speech that could be r ad both ways. I thought at first that he was go ng to enunciate a new policy and that we w 're not going to be so very far away on quest, ons of tariff policy. I thought that when ne was advocating a policy for the great west he was recanting somewhat his own attitude in 1924 when we brought in a tariff policy we thought was of great advantage to the west.

Let the hon. gentleman
speak for the Liberal party, not for the Conservative party.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I discovered that my hon.
friend had not introduced any new tariff policy, but simply the old tariff policy of 1908 -adequate protection with a new turn to it, so that hon. gentlemen opposite could use it in any part of the country.
Now I come to the observations of the hon. member for Macleod regarding the income tax, and I am going to remind my hon. friends again of the reductions that were made last year as applied to the earned, income, the reductions that wiped out the income tax altogether as regards many people throughout this country. My hon. friend was in the House and he will recall that I was attacked, as I have been in some degree this year, for having increased the taxes on many; and it is true we did. But my hon. friend
argues that the income tax in all oases is a direct tax. I admit that to a considerable degree the income tax is a direct tax, that impression prevails throughout the country; but when you look carefully into the figures, as I have had the opportunity of doing, and look carefully into the sources from which we get this taxation, it will be discovered that it is not altogether direct tax. When I say that I want hon. gentlemen to keep in mind that what I am going to say now applies to all the provinces of Canada. In the year I am quoting we received something over $55,000,000 of income tax. Hon. gentlemen may be surprised to know that of that $55,000,000 over $31,000,000 was paid in by 5,738 corporations. Now you may argue as you like, but the corporations will pass that tax back to the consumers somewhere. In Prince Edward Island there were 42. of these corporations, in Nova Scotia, 220, in New Brunswick, 220, in Quebec, 1,159, in Ontario, 2,397, in Manitoba, 481, in Saskatchewan, 226, in Alberta, 282, in British Columbia, 702, and in Yukon, 5. These corporations contributed in the aggregate oveT $31,000,000 of the $55,000,000 collected.

Will the minister
permit a question?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes.

I presume the tax of
which he is speaking, namely, the income tax upon corporations, is a tax imposed on profits that have been earned and declared.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes.

Will the minister
kindly explain how such a corporation, paying that tax after its profits have been made and declared, passes that tax on to the consumer?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Every corporation, like every business man, plays safe, and takes profits enough to provide for insurance, wear and tear, and the general conduct of the business. That is my answer.

Is not that answer
based on theory and not on practice?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I am not disposed to enter
into an argument with my hon. friend. I have simply stated the fact that out of the $55,000,000 of income tax collected more than half of it was paid by corporations and not by individuals.

Should not the minister be careful not to make the statement that a corporation necessarily passes that tax on to the consumer without knowing the facts?
The Budget-Mr. Robb

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
If my hon. friend thinks that the corporations are philanthropists he entertains a different view from what I do.
Now, my hon. friend the official leader of the opposition did give some reasons this afternoon for the opposition which he and his party presented to the budget brought down in 1924 when we made such sweeping reductions, particularly on agricultural implements and on the implements and tools required by the farmer, the lumberman, and oie miner. He told us this afternoon that there were many members on that side who were now astonished at the size of the west. We on this side were not astonished at the size of the west. We knew of the size of the west, and it was because we believed that a really national policy for Canada was one that would appeal to western Canada, that in 1924 we braved the opposition of hon. gentlemen opposite and reduced the duties to such an extent on agricultural implements. This afternoon my hon. friend argued first that there should be greater immigration into this country. Then he proceeded to tell us of the great harm we had done to the producers on the land because we reduced the duties on agricultural implements. The inference was that if he was returned to power, he would increase the duties and so he would induce people to come to Canada by charging them more for the agricultural implements which they required to purchase.

Surely the minister will
agree that the leader of the opposition pointed out that before this government reduced the duties, the prices of agricultural implements were lowered.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I know the hon. gentleman
argued that by our reducing the tariff the price of implements was increased. The only conclusion possible is that if you want cheaper implements, you must put the tariff up higher.

As a purchaser of farm implements I would ask the minister if he can name one implement of the farm to-day that can be purchased cheaper because of the minister's reduction in the duty on farm implements?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
That proves that my hon.
friend was voicing the sentiment of his subordinates in that they desire a higher tariff in order to get cheaper implements.
A tariff that will protect.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
My hon. friend said that we
took good care not to reduce the duty on boots and shoes-

Mr. Speaker,-
	i ,	; J
Sit down.
Order.

An hon. gentleman who is held in such high esteem in this House as the Minister of Finance is expected to answer questions so as to enable members to understand the situation. Is it not a fact that the real argument of the leader of the opposition was that the tariff was not the determining factor in the fixing of prices, but that prices were fixed by other factors? Is the minister fair in stating the matter in the way he did?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Why then should my hon.
friend have devoted, as he did, twenty minutes of his speech to attacking this government for having reduced tariffs? The official speaker for the opposition said that we took good care not to reduce the duty on boots and shoes. Was that intended as a preparation for the next campaign, or was it an attack on his former leader and on all speeches made on that side of the House during the past two years? Because we have been accused in this House by hon. members opposite of having ruined the boot and shoe industry of Canada. I can recall when we spent long days and nights here listening to speeches of hon. gentlemen opposite who accused us of having reduced the duty on boots and shoes and of having thereby ruined the boot and shoe industry of this country.
I must keep my promise not to detain the House at any great length.

Will the minister, before
he concludes, be good enough to allow me. a question?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes.

Will the minister kindly
explain his announcements: first, of April. 1924, of $20,000,000; second, of March, 1925, of $35,000,000; third, of April 15, 1926, of $22,000,000, and fourth, of February 7, 1927, of $31,000,000, a total of about $110,000,000, in each case announced as a reduction in the public debt? On Friday evening at
nine o'clock the hon. member for Argenteuil (Sir George Perley) was discussing the bill respecting the Montreal, Ottawa and Georgian Bay Canal Company, and the hour for the consideration of private bills expiring then, he resumed his seat without making a motion to adjourn the debate. Nothing in the rules of the House, nor in the precedents, usages and customs of parliament, required him to
make such a motion. My attention on that evening was directed to the fact that the hon. member had made no motion to adjourn the debate. I thereupon consulted Bourinot and the precedents cited by him at the foot of page 227 of the fourth edition. I discovered to my great surprise that many years ago, possibly twenty-five years since, I piloted a bill through the House when the same situation arose. That bill related to the Hull Electric Railway, and on the hour for the discussion of private bills expiring, it automatically went over to the next day allotted to such bills, no motion having been necessary for the adjournment of the debate in that case. The circumstance is cited by Bourinot at the page I have mentioned. Bourinot says:
If a private bill is under consideration on Tuesday and Fridays, after eight o'clock and the debate is not concluded thereon at nine, a member may call the attention of the Speaker to the fact that the hour allotted to such subjects under the rules has expired, and the question will thereupon go over until another day, when it will be taken up at the same stage where its progress was interrupted.
The cases cited under that dictum of Bourinot are to be found in Canadian Commons Journals, 1896, second session, 105, 112, Hull Electric Railway, and also in the year 1899, 106, 118 and 119, Ontario and Rainy River Railway. The same point presented itself in the year 1898.
Of course, I perceive the anomaly of the situation, and I cannot help wishing that there were a positive rule governing such cases. Every hon. member will readily understand that one contentious bill arising in this way might obstruct the passage of a whole series of others following it, and that is what is happening in this instance. The only thing I see to be done, as has been done to my knowledge before, is for the House to favour an agreement between the contending factions in order to let the business of the House proceed regularly, or take upon itself to let unopposed bills pass first. When there is a conflict of opinion as between the various parliamentary authorities, the Speaker may seek the judgment of the House. In the present instance there is on one side Bourinot and the precedents cited by the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Cahan) when the question was not raised in the House but was decided by the Clerk. Then, as against Bourinot, there is the present Clerk of the House of Commons, who, in paragraph 323 under rule 33, says:

Its purpose is to keep the motion on the order paper though on Wednesday the House may rise without debate being adjourned because at six o'clock on that day the Speaker adjourns the House without question put. On other days, if debate is not adjourned the question is superseded.
That is to say, according to Beauchesne, the question under discussion loses its place and goes to the bottom of the list. MONTREAL, OTTAWA AND GEORGL\N BAY CANAL COMPANY
The House resumed from Friday, February 25, consideration of the motion of Mr. Chevrier for the seicond reading of Bill No. 78, respecting the Montreal, Ottawa and Georgian Bay Canal Company.

subtopic: PRECEDENCE OP MOTION UNDISPOSED OB' ON EXPIRY OF HOUR FOR PRIVATE BILLS
speechtext:
May I say in opening that the hon. member for Ottawa (Mr. Chevrier) is an old friend of mine, and I am rather surprised to have him accuse me of not playing fair. I do not suppose he really meant it in the strict sense of the word, but it seems to me that those promoting the bills which follow this might accuse even my hon. friend of a lack of fair play. I do not consider this a private bill in the ordinary sense of the word. Private bills come here in large numbers at every session, and in most cases they deal with incorporations or alterations of charters of companies really of a private nature, but in actual practice this is a public affair having to do with the building of the Georgian Bay canal. Although it is classified as a private bill, my reason for speaking now is because I consider this actually a bill having very much to do with the public. I therefore think it only right that hon. members of thi3 House who live far away should be informed of the facts in regard to this matter. So far as I am concerned I have no expectation or idea of trying to keep this bill from going to committee; we all know very well that cannot be done and we have no wish to do so. We do wish, however, to have it fully discussed here before going to committee in order that it may be thoroughly understood by everyone.
When speaking the other evening I gave the House a brief history of the Georgian Bay canal according to my memory, and I was in Ottawa during that time and in the House for many years when this was then under discussion. I desire to say now, Mr. Speaker, that conditions in Canada have changed tremendously in the last thirty years; we have a new generation, and in many ways it is not *the same world at all that it was in 1894. At that time the first bill having to do with this canal was promoted and passed in this House, and at that time very few of us had any idea that wateir-power would become of such great value. I know more or less about the various waterfalls of the Ottawa river, and it is fifty years since I saw some of those above Pembroke, and at that time the only thing in our minds was how difficult these waterfalls made the bringing down of

Georgian Bay Canal Company
our logs and timber. No one had any idea whatever, and there was no suggestion, that these water-powers would some day become a vast source not only of wealth but of comfort to the people of Canada. Now everything is different. There has been a tremendous development in water-power since discoveries have been made as to how best to use electricity or the power that is generated. In fact I may say without exaggeration that water power and the electricity generated from it constitute really the lifeblood of this country. We have many industries here that could not exist without water-power, and it is specially valuable in this northern country where we have a cold winter, and particularly in the centre of Canada where there are no visible supplies of coal. These water-powers provide us with our white coal, and I do not think I am exaggerating when I express my honest belief, in view of the progress of electrical development, that we or our children will see the time when we shall use it not only for power but for heating our houses thus taking the place of those vast quantities of coal that we import from the United States every year and pay for with our good money
Now the Georgian Bay canal charter gives to the compaSy certain water rights. I am not a lawyer but I find these rights ill defined and their meaning very difficult to grasp, and there are certain contingent rights provided for. The question of the relationship of the Dominion and the provinces with regard to water and water-powers has been under discussion off and on during all the years since confederation. I believe it is generally conceded now, that the provinces own the land under the water and the water that run3 down the streams, with the sole exception that the Dominion has a paramount right for navigation purposes and for navigation purposes only. In building a canal, which the Dominion government has the right to do, they have to use a certain amount of water, and they are entitled to take that amount of water but no more. I think that if this charter is to be continued it should be made perfectly plain what water rights it purports to grant, and to confine them entirely and strictly to water that is required for canal purposes.
I notice that when the newspapers and individuals also have discussed this question of late they are apt to refer to Carillon power; they talk about the Carillon problem and the Carillon question as if that were the only one at issue. I have heard people say: Why this is a matter between a company in Montreal and the Georgian Bay Canal Company. As a matter of fact, Mr. Speaker, the site of
the Carillon water-power is in the county of Argenteuil which I have the honour to represent, and we want that power developed as soon as possible. People down there have been looking forward for years to the development of this power in order to bring industry there and to afford employment to the residents. They are tired of waiting for its realization, and I do not blame them. I may say that to my surprise in the election of 1925 one of the gentlemen from Montreal who was interested in the lease of the Carillon power given to them by the Department of Railways and Canals came into the county of Argenteuil and opposed me very strongly on the ground that I had not done enough to help on the development of this water-power. Now that all originated from the fact that at that time there was a lot of discussion as to whether the power, after being developed, could be exported or not. I am not going to go all over that question because it has nothing to do with the point I am trying to make this evening, but I want +' ^ay that people down there are not much interested as to what company develops the Carillon waterpower. They simply wish the development to be carried out and carried out as quickly as possible, but on the distinct understanding that there shall be no authority to export the power after it has been developed. I mention this because the reference in the newspapers, and by individuals, to the Carillon waterpower is very misleading.
I want the House to understand that although the Carillon water-power is a large one it is only one of many. There are a dozen or more water-powers on the Ottawa river as large or nearly as large as the Carillon water-power. So that the Georgian Bay canal project, although discussed as having reference solely to the Carillon waterpower, really refers to all these water-powers on the Ottawa river and on the Mattawa and French rivers as well. The Ottawa river has an immense capacity for water-power; It has been estimated at well over a million horse-power. That is the quantity of power which we are considering to-night if the Georgian Bay Canal Company has any authority in regard to developing the same. The Ottawa river is practically a succession of lakes and rapids, so that a good head can be obtained at eight or ten different points on that river at each of which a very large quantity of horse-power can be developed. In addition to the Ottawa river there are the Mattawa river and the French river. They are not as large streams as the Ottawa but still up towards the height of land the fall is great and consequently they are valuable
Georgian Bay Canal Company

also from the point of view of power development. I only mention these facts to show to you that in considering this question we are not considering merely one water-power, or any dispute there may be between two companies. As to the latter point I have nothing to do whatever, but I do say that if the charter of the Georgian Bay Canal Company is going to be extended it should be definitely stated in it that the company have no right to any water except what is required for canal purposes.
Some people say: Why, we can get the canal without any cost if the power rights go with it. The canal can be built and the water-powers developed without any cost to anybody if these rights go together. I claim that that is a confusion of ideas: it is not a fair way to put it, and the argument cannot be maintained. No one can build a canal without cost, and if the power rights are to be used for that purpose, and the value of the power is to be used to pay for the cost of building a canal it means that the power developed will bear the cost of the canal and the power users will have to pay for it. If this canal is going to be built, either by this company or by any other company, the project should be considered on its merits. If the canal is still required in the interests of the trade of this country, it should not be mixed up with the power development, nor should users of power in Ontario and Quebec be called upon practically to pay for the canal. Moreover, if the idea, could be carried out, that is if the power development and the canal scheme were combined, and the profit on the power used to build the canal, that would to my mind infringe upon provincial rights and deprive the people of those provinces of the cheap light, heat and power which they so much need. If the water^powers were developed on their merits without any reference to the canal, our peotple would secure this cheap light, heat and power which, as I said before, is so vital to their prosperity and comfort.
If the power and the canal scheme were to be developed each on its own merits, this could he done only with the cooperation of the provinces and by arrangement with them. Last Friday evening, when I was discussing this matter, I said that I had no objection to any group of men spending their money to build the Georgian Bay canal if they saw fit to do so. I did not mean- by that that they should use the profits from the power development to build the -canal. If they are going to build the canal they should build it at their own cost, and my contention is that under present conditions this is something they will never do.

I said the other evening and I reiterate that I do not consider this in any sense a party question, and I hope it will not be taken up in any such spirit. As a matter of fact I have looked over the list of -directors, the last named in this series of fourteen different bills renewing the charter of this company, and I find there are five gentlemen, two of whom are old friends of mine and Conservatives, one is a Liberal and I do not know what the politics of the other two are. Those are the men who are put down as directors. As to who at present controls the charter, I do not know and I have not been informed. Rumour is busy regarding this and perhaps I may be allowed to read an extract from an article in the Citizen of the 7th September last, dealing with this subject. The article reads:
The situation must be frankly recognized, however: there would be no economic justification for building the Georgian bay canal at this time. There is no lack of transportation lines for the grain movement. There is congestion in the port of Montreal when the harvest begins to pour down from the west, but another canal would contribute nothing towards the solution of Montreal's problem.
The Canadian people own a magnificent railway line from Winnipeg to the port of Quebec, the National Transcontinental, which is far from being adequately used. It would he more economical to fix a rate for grain transportation on the National Transcontinental to compete with lake shipping rates, than to build another competitive canal.
There is no remote likelihood that the interests behind Mr. Sifton would put money into the construction of any such canal. But it is quite likely that money would be forthcoming to set up a great hydro-electric power monopoly, privately controlled, along the route of the Georgian bay canal.
Mr. Sifton might as well realize that the day has gone by in Canada when public opinion would allow that monopoly to be established. The people of Ontario have reason to know the value of hydro-electric power resources. Public ownership has given this province an unrivalled electric service. People in other parts of Canada are similarly awakening to the advantages of public ownership of public utilities.
Private enterprise on the Georgian hay canal is just about twenty years behind the times. The canal may he built some day. It would contribute to the industrial development of the country of which Ottawa is the commercial hub. But no government could long survive the storm which would properly rise in Canada if it were to fall in with the plans of Mr. Sifton.
That is from the Ottawa Citizen of September 7, 1926, a paper that is certainly not considered as supporting the Conservative side of politics. I am sorry the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Stewart) is not in his seat. Last year the question of the St. Lawrence canal project was being discussed in this House for quite a length of time, and I was pleased at

Georgian Bay Canal Company
that time to find t'he Minister of the Interior so frank in his statement of the situation. If I may be permitted, I wish to read a couple of extracts from what he said on that occasion. This is what the minister said in April, 1926, as reported on page 2192 of the revised Hansard:
May I say that there is no dispute so far as this government is concerned with respect to the ownership of the water-powers, or no dispute as to the ownership of the bed of the streams out to the point where the international boundary intervenes. So far as I know this government have never raised any question as to ownership. Nor does this government raise any question as to the right of Ontario to develop that particular power or any power along that reach.
That acknowledges the right of Ontario in the water as fully as anybody could acknowledge it, but there is more. On page 2194 of the revised Hansard the Minister of the Interior says further:
I wish again to emphasize the fact that we are in entire agreement -with the Ontario government. There is no dispute about their ownership of the power or the land to the international boundary. If they want to develop there would be no holdup, so far as the federal government is concerned. I should like to see the hydro development on the Ottawa river.
Mark you, the Ottawa river.
It seems to me there is a great opportunity for such development there. However, they have set their hearts on the development of the St. Lawrence, and it is the business of this government to do everything they can to facilitate that development.
From that I take it that it would be impossible for the Minister of the Interior to support this Georgian Bay canal bill. I appeal to him on the basis of his words of last year to support those of us who do not think the Georgian Bay Canal Company should receive any rights to water except what they require for canal purposes. The other day the minister waxed quite indignant with the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens) when the old problem about the export of Carillon power was under discussion. Therefore, if the minister were in his seat, I would say to him: I take it for granted that you will support those who are opposed to the renewal of this charter in its present form. Further than that, I take it that the government cannot support this bill without violating the resolution Which they agreed to last year. This is the resolution which was being debated and regarding which the minister made the remarks that I have quoted:
That in the opinion of this House, the government of Ontario and the Hydro Electric Power Commission of Ontario should be given leave
forthwith to develop and generate power on the St. Lawrence river at what is known as the Morrisburg dam, and should also be given power to use an increased flow of water from the Niagara river-
And so forth. That will be found in Hansard of 1926 on page 2182. The resolution goes on to say:
-and that this House will support the government in taking such immediate action as herein proposed without further delays in accordance with the application of the Ontario government.
I am very happy to find, Sir, these quotations of what was said by the minister, and also the views of the government as expressed in this resolution. But, Mr. Speaker, I would like to know whether the promoters of this bill really intend to build a canal or not. The reason I ask that is that I find at the end of the first section of the proposed bill the following words:
-or if the said canals are not completed and put in operation within the said periods respectively, the powers granted to the company by parliament shall cease and be null and void, as respects so much of the said canals and works as then remains uncompleted.
In other words, if the government were dissatisfied with the way the company was carried on they might develop a water-power and not build a canal at all, and all the government could do would be to say: Well, that is not satisfactory; it is not in accordance with your contract. Under the clause as it is worded here the company would then claim that they had a right to keep the works they had already developed. I cannot see the object of putting that in at all. It seems to me a most dangerous clause, and I think it should be altered when the bill is taken up in committee.
But that is not all. Apart from the important question of water and water powers, I would ask this House, what about public ownership? In 1894 public ownership was not a vital question in Canada, but it is today. We have embarked upon two of the greatest public ownership enterprises in any country in the world. We have our national railways, and we have a free system of canals. Thirty years ago tolls were charged on the canals, but there are none now on the government canals. Is there any member of this House who is a believer in public ownership who could vote to renew this charter for the Georgian Bay Canal Company, which is empowered to charge tolls on the canal on the Ottawa river? Is that consistent with the feeling of those who are in favour of public ownership? Are we going to have the Do-
Georgian Bay Canal Company

minion government canals, built by the people of Canada, free, and at the same time have tolls charged on the Georgian Bay canal, built by a private company? It would simply mean that our railways would have a competing water system, run by a private company, and authorized to charge tolls. If this matter of building a canal is going to be considered, it seems to me that the work ought to be undertaken by the Dominion government itself. They ought to consider the question on its own merits.
Furthermore, if this charter is going to be renewed I submit to hon. members that it should be entirely redrafted to suit modern conditions. Here is a charter thirty-three years old which has been amended fourteen times, so much so that it is very difficult for anybody to go through it and find out just what powers are being granted. I take it, in view of the development of water-powers and of public ownership at the present time, that parliament would not consider the granting of a charter such as this, giving the company control of an enterprise of this huge size with all the water-power on the Ottawa river. Why should they suggest that we renew a charter by means of this simple bill? If the company think they should have their charter extended, why do they not bring in a new bill, with clauses to meet present-day conditions, so that parliament may consider it as it would the bill of any other company that comes here for legislation?
This Georgian Bay Canal Company has no rights on account of what they have done, for they have done nothing. They spent some money on surveys and so on, but they have not done any work for all these thirty-three years, and my own feeling is that this charter should not be renewed at all. But if it is going to be renewed, care should be taken to see that it is brought up to date, and particularly that clauses are inserted confining the use of water to canal purposes alone.
There is a clause in the charter, which will be found in chapter 128 of 6 Edward VII, assented to on July 13, 1906, under which the ivorks may be taken over by the government. It reads as follows:
His Majesty, his heirs and successors, may at any time assume the possession of, and the property in, the said canals and works, and of and in all the rights, privileges and advantages of the company on giving to the company one week's notice of intention to do so; and thereupon all property in the said canals, works, rights, privileges and advantages shall become, and thenceforward shall be, vested in His Majesty, his heirs and successors, and by way of compensation His Majesty shall pay to the company the value of the work actually done by
[Sir George Perley.j
the company up to the time of the giving of such notice in surveying, and in the making of plans, and otherwise upon the ground, together with the value of all tangible property of the company of which possession may be so taken,- such values to be fixed by three valuators, or the majority of them, one valuator to be chosen by His Majesty, another by the company, and the third by the two so chosen.
In my judgment the proper way to deal with this question is for the government to allow the charter to lapse and then deal with the matter under this clause. I cannot see that it would do any harm to the shareholders, and it would give the government a free hand to work together with the provinces in this matter on a reasonable basis. I may say-
