subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when the House rose at six o'clock I was about to bring to its attention a case of discriminatory taxation which has prevailed in the province of Quebec for now some ten years. A great number of the citizens, not only of the province of Quebec, but undoubtedly many others throughout Canada who have the interests of just taxation at heart, desire that a remedy should be provided in this case. I have reference to section 5 (c) of the Income Tax Act of 1917, which provides that:
The income of any company, commission or association not less than ninety per cent of the stock or capital of which is owned by a province or a municipality,
-shall not be liable to taxation under the act. It so happens, Mr. Speaker, that in the province of Quebec we have followed the rule of having our public utilities conducted by private companies. In that regard we differ

The Budget-Mr. Bell (St. Antoine)
to a great extent from the other provinces, and it is a well-known fact that ninety-five per cent of the public utilities in the province of Quebec are private corporations. In order that this matter may be brought to the attention of the government and that the government may have a full record of the campaign that has been taking place for a number of years, I intend to burden the House to-night by putting on record extracts from different newspapers in that province, Liberal, Conservative and Independent, and also from different associations which have no politics, such as boards of trade and chambers of commerce, in order to bear out the assertion that some remedy is required immediately regarding this unjust taxation.
It was stated by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) this afternoon that the corporations of this country pay some fifty-five per cent of the income tax, and it was further stated that a great amount of the income tax is in the final stages paid by the consumer. On that point especially as to public utilities, I think the facts will bear him out and will prove that that assertion is correct. For instance, the Montreal Light, Heat and Power Company, which owns the public utilities of heat and power in the city of Montreal paid an income tax last year of $783,000, and also the Montreal Tramways Company, another public utility paying a tax of almost $125,000, all of which in the end is a burden upon the consumers of gas and electricity and in the second instance, upon those who use the street cars in the city of Montreal.
I quote first of all from La Presse, which is well known to be a French newspaper, independent in politics, and having one of the largest circulations of any newspaper in Canada. La Presse of February 10 publishes the following:
A flagrant injustice is committed in the distinction that is drawn by the federal treasury in the matter of the income tax levy between private corporations that produce electric light and energy and companies of the same kind that operate under provincial and municipal control. This difference of treatment creates a prejudice against the customers of the private companies and concedes a favour to consumers who obtain their service from government-controlled concerns. If a company has to pay $700,000 or $800,000 a year in income tax, the price of the products of that company must necessarily be calculated in a manner that will repay that sum. The customers, therefore, will be charged from $700,000 to $800,000 a year more for what they buy than they would otherwise have to pay, whilst the clients of companies under government control are liberated from this surcharge. In the province of Quebec we have refused to submit to the municipalization system which has infatuated certain other provinces, and all things considered there is no
need to regret our attitude. In any event, it is our incontestable right to prefer the system of private ownership of our electric light and power services, and the federal government has no right to favor one system more than another. Its absolute and strict duty is to put everybody, every enterprise and every province on one and the same fiscal footing. At the present time, however, as regards the income tax, the federal administration, ceding to strange considerations, has failed to obey this rule of elementary justice. Well, let us leave out the past. Let us pass the sponge over the influences or considerations that have been responsible for this denial of fiscal justice, insupportable by the consumers in the province of Quebec who have been obliged to pay into the Dominion treasury for electric light, and energy surcharge, which their neighbors in Ontario do not have to pay. Let us overlook what is past and simply say that this denial of justice cannot continue. The government ought to apply the remedy without further delay; and we hope that parliament will take up the question.
We pass now to the Montreal Gazette, a leading English daily, and it also calls for redress of this unjust taxation. In its issue of February 11 that paper says:
The inequitable incidence of the income tax as between publicly and privately owned public utilities is again a subject of discussion, and the consideration that is being given to it is timely and proper. It would be a good thing for the Dominion, and by no means a bad thing for the government, if this tax were abolished altogether; but, if that is not to be done, there should at least be such revision as will prevent discrimination as between one group of citizens and another, or between one province and another. Equity is, or ought to be, a first principle in all taxation measures, and economists have always agreed that a tax which is not levied impartially is vicious and cannot be successfully defended.
Under the present system, the income tax is collected from private companies which sell electrical energy for lighting and power purposes, while similar services, when provided under government or municipal ownership or control, are not taxed. The tax, when imposed, is collected from the companies, but is paid in the last instance by their customers, the consumers of light and power. It so happens that this discrimination places the Ontario consumer in one class and the Quebec consumer in another, power and light services being publicly owned in Ontario and privately owned in this province. Parliament did not set out to differentiate in this way as between one province and another, but that is the way it works out, and it is a matter of some importance in considering the principle involved. The consumer in Quebec is affected adversely in that the income tax, when added to the actual price of power and light, lessens the advantage which private enterprise and efficiency confers upon its customers. This is a matter of first-rate importance from the standpoint of the community as well as from that of the individual, since cheap power and cheap light have become determining factors in the field of industrial expansion. Light and power costs, nowadays, attract new industries or encourage the extension of existing industries, when these



The Budget-Mr. Bell (St. Antoine)
costs are low; and, this being so, it is clearly necessary to the economic progress of Montreal that light and power costs should not be burdened with charges that are not imposed upon similar services in other parts of Canada.
The remedy is simple. Either parliament should tax all light and power services equally, whether they be publicly or privately owned, or all should be exempted. Consumers in Quebec ask for no favors in this respect, but they are entitled to fair treatment and should have it. If the government and parliament come to the conclusion that the tax cannot be collected from publicly-owned services, owing to the conditions of financing and bookkeeping that are peculiar to this field of public ownership, there is still the alternative method of making the exemption general. The existing situation is grossly unfair to consumers and consuming communities in this province, and it calls for redress.
La Presse of about the same date again
states:
We consider it to be of urgent importance that public opinion should be couvinccd of the disadvantages which, economically, result from this vicious practice. We have already called attention to its evident consequences to the consumers, clients of the private companies, who must necessarily reimburse the amount levied upon the corporations. In this way the consumers lose part of the natural benefit that otherwise would come to them from the economic results of private administration, which assures the lowest cost price. But this is not the only disadvantage that is caused by this fiscal injustice, particularly in Montreal. However important may be the private interest of each consumer, we must not forget to take into account the general interest as well, the higher interest of the community. Indeed the one canuot be separated from the other. Everybody knows that whatever will aid the industrial and commercial development of a city, will also advance the welfare of the citizens. The question of the cost of light and power is one of capital importance in all industrial and commercial matters. Whoever proposes to set up a new industrial installation must calculate with great care the expenses that will have to be incurred under this head, and, all other things being equal, he will instal his industry in the city where light, heat and power are to be obtained at the lowest rates. Consequently, we all, as citizens of Montreal, have the greatest interest to protest against a fiscal injustice which risks injury to the economic development of the city.
We suggested the other day that, as a means to end the actual inequality of treatment, the government should either tax the municipalized and provincial government-controlled enterprises . on the same basis as the private companies, or else exempt the latter as the others are already exempted. But, as a matter of fact, the first alternative does not appear to be practicable, for the good and sufficient reason that the municipalized and government-controlled enterprises, having either the province or the municipality as their money-lenders, and consequently not having to trouble about meeting the interest charges on the capital-the people pay this piper-matters can be so arranged that there is no apparent balance at the end of the fiscal year. Having, therefore, no

apparent revenue they as it were, automatically find themselves exempt from the tax on revenue. It is a piece of legerdemain too easy to perform. The only practical solution, then, would be to exempt private corporations from the income tax just as the municipalized, government-controlled enterprises are exempted to-day.-
I also quote an extract from La Patrie another French Conservative newspaper in Montreal, in its leading editorial of February 14 last, complaining of this million dollars taken unjustly in the way of income tax from public utilities privately owned in the province of Quebec. It says:
A tax which is unjust because of the inequality of its application is the income tax on private companies of public.utility whilst similar enterprises under municipal or provincial government control are allowed to go scot free. In this way the distribution of electric light and power in Montreal, and the tramways service in the same city are heavily taxed-the amount being about $1,000,000 a year-but Toronto and towns and cities in Ontario pay no contribution under this head. Montrealers are not opposed to the tax, but they do protest against its inequality: The government at Ottawa has for several years past remained deaf to the supplications from Montreal and the province of Quebec asking that this injustice shall come to an end.
I also direct the attention of the government to a letter addressed to the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) by the Montreal Board of Trade under date of March 22 last, as follows:
The council of this board has the honour to remind you of the injustice involved in the present application to Public Utilities of the Income Tax Act in that citizens served by privately owned utilities are made subject to a federal tax from which citizens served by publicly owned utilities are free.
The council wrote you on this subject on 25th September, 1924, but we have heard of no action to remove the grievance. That letter made special reference to the discrimination against the citizens of Montreal, customers of the Montreal Light, Heat and Power Company. That company will pay into the federal exchequer as income tax on its profits for 1925 the sum of $783,000, all taken out of the pockets of its customers. All other citizens of the Dominion served by privately owned utilities are similarly penalized but, since about 95 per cent of electrical energy in the province of Quebec is produced by privately owned companies, the discrimination against the citizens of this province, and in favour of those of provinces where public ownership is the rule, is as serious as it is indefensible.
The council realizes the need for federal revenues and does not ask relief for the citizens of this province, but it does wish to renew its protest against the existing discrimination.
The council respectfully renews its suggestion that the income tax on public utilities be based in future, not on profits but on gross revenue, and that it be applicable alike to all utilities, whether publicly or privately owned.

The Budget-Mr. Bell (St. Antoine)

speechtext:
I will cpme to that in a moment.
The council ventures to urge that this matter is of sufficient importance to call for remedial legislation at the present session of parliament.
I have the honour to be, Sir,
Your obedient servant,
J. Stanley Cook,
Secretary.
That is from the Montreal Board of Trade, a body composed of representative business men of that city, without any political axes to grind, and who take a very lively interest in the progress of the city. Naturally they want to see Montreal given equal treatment with any other city in the Dominion.
I come now to the Chambre de Commerce, a body similar to the board of trade but composed principally of French citizens from every walk of life in Montreal. On February 23 these representative men accepted the following resolution from the legislation committee:
Whereas public utilities in some provinces are directed by private companies;
Whereas those companies pay high income tax;
Whereas those taxes always fall ultimately upon the consumer;
Whereas public utilities in other provinces are not taxed because they are publicly owned;
Whereas this discrimination is an encouragement for the installation of new industries in sister provinces, but is a hindrance to Quebec;
Whereas, if more equally applied, tlie tax would bring greater returns;
It is resolved that the federal government be asked to refrain from imposing income tax on public utility companies and that, if need be, the tax in question be replaced by another tax which would be applicable to all public utilities without discrimination for any province.
Next I have here a resolution passed at the fourth annual convention of the Canadian Tax and Civil Service Research Conference of the Citizens' Research Institute of Canada, held in Winnipeg <xn September 28 and 29, 1926. This is a Dominion-wide institution with head offices in Toronto and branches in all the important cities in Canada from coast to coast. Resolution No. 5 as passed by them reads:
Be it resolved that this convention urges the taxation of all public utilities on the same basis, irrespective of ownership, public or private.
I come now to the question asked by the hon. member for North Winnipeg (Mr. Heaps).as to whether privately owned utility companies charge the same rates as those charged by publicly owned companies. Let
me quote from the ninth annual report of Montreal Light, Heat and Power Consolidated :	*
The taxation of your company is excessively heavy and openly discriminatory, as our operations are subject to heavy federal income taxes, whereas the provincial and municipal undertakings of Ontario and other provinces, although on a similar commercial basis, not only enjoy immunity from provincial and municipal taxation. but under the federal law are exempted entirely from income taxation.
Incidentally your company will this year pay the federal exchequer approximately $783,000 for income tax on its business for 1925, which, of course, is included in our rates for service and suggests if there were no income tax to pay our present retail rate of 3J cents per k.w.h. for electricity could be reduced to 2.88 cents per k.w.h., or, if applied to our gas business, the present retail rate of $1.10 per thousand cubic feet could be reduced to 91 cents per thousand feet.
It is significant, as stated, that consumers of electricity in Ontario and other provinces where utilities are publicly owned are exempt from this taxation. Our consumers, we are sure, do not object to paying their proportion of the running expenses of the country; they do, however, object (and rightly so) to paying the proportion of Toronto, Winnipeg and other cities where the utilities are publicly owned and operated. Our protestations, as well as the able and well defined representations of the Montreal Board of Trade to tlie federal government, anent this question have so far been without avail, and your directors feel that the consumers of electricity in this province should take some more effectual steps to correct this discrimination. Meantime this open discrimination in taxation undoubtedly handicaps Montreal and the province of Quebec.
The continued increase in the disbursements for taxes-municipal, provincial t '	-
reflect the national situation with rt the present habit of lavish expenditures by governmental agencies. It is a question that calls for serious individual thought when a business such as yours, furnishing public necessities, is called upon to disburse in taxes the sum of $1,274,655.56, upwards of 19 per cent of the company's net income.
These are the points I wished to bring to the attention of the House with reference to the taxation of public utilities in the province of Quebec and particularly in the city of Montreal. As I have already pointed out there is an extra charge levied on the consumers of both gas and electricity which would be considerably reduced if it were not necessary to pay th'is federal tax.
There is an even more serious aspect than that, however; in the development of the province we must at all costs be protected from competition with cur sister provinces, particularly in the securing of industries. As the public utilities are at present discriminated against, we often find that we have lost industries from our provinces because of the fact that cheaper power can be obtained in
772	COMMONS
The Budget-Mr. Bell (St. Antoine)
neighbouring provinces. I wish it made perfectly clear that we in Quebec and in the city of Montreal are not asking that taxation be increased in any other province; we are only asking for fair play to the public utilities in our own province. For example, it has been pointed out by some of these newspaper reports that there should be a tax levied upon the gross revenue. That appears practically impossible in regard to the public utilities of Ontario, and therefore we would ask for the same treatment accorded to other municipalized and government controlled utility companies; that this tax be removed and the income tax be not applied.
It may seem rather strange that a member of the opposition should take up this matter on behalf of the public utilities of Quebec, because one would think that the interests of that province would be well looked after by those on the government benches. We on this side of the House from Quebec number only four as compared with sixty-one on the opposite side, including a number of outstanding ministers of the crown who know of this unjust taxation. One might have expected them to pass some remedial legislation to correct this abuse, which has undoubtedly been drawn to their attention in different ways, but that has not yet been done. I hope it is not too late for this corrective legislation to be passed this session and I trust that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) whom we know to be a native of Quebec, will take the course which is undoubtedly open to him in order to remedy this grievance. I am sure those from other provinces are fairminded in these matters, and that they wish taxation to be at least fair; I do not think they want to see one province discriminated against in the matter of taxation or placed at a disadvantage in the securing of industries.
That, Mr. Speaker, is all I had intended to say, except to mention the fact that I am sorry that it was not possible in the present budget to make some amendment to the '.ncome tax laws in favour of those who contribute to charities. In the very large cities as well as in the towns there is a constant call for funds for charitable purposes, and I trust that in the next budget some consideration will be given to this question. We find it extremely difficult to finance our great charitable institutions which relieve distressed people; people are continually asked for contributions, and I think they might well be exempted for the amount they contribute in that way.
[Mr. L. G. Bell.l
Before closing I would like to refer to the remarks of the hon. member for Saskatoon (Mr. Young), who unfortunately is not in his seat, having particular reference to his remarks regarding the tariff board. I trust that whatever may be the personal views of different members of this House, we can all take a large national view of this matter, more so than the view I understood the hon. member to express. I will repeat what he stated:
I wish, however, to be on record as saying that if at any time that board is to be used as an instrument or agent to hide behind in order to increase the tariff, I would say: Get thee gone and give way to honest men. We can never give the functions of this House over to that tariff board or to any other tariff board that may be created. I want to be perfectly frank in that regard.
I think it would be of very little use, as an hon. member urged the day following, for any of us to attend the meetings of this board if that is to be the attitude of the board; we might as well stay at home and not try to present the case for an increase ol the tariff. I am sure the hon. member was not in earnest wThen he stated that- the tariff board has been created by this government to decrease the tariff only; we would rather look at it as a board which will see to it in all cases that justice is done, whatever the issue.
I also wish to refer to the remarks of the hon. member for Maple Creek (Mr. Spence) in which he says:
We believe in freedom of trade as a principle because we know that the whole trend of modern times is towards the great field of internationalism-not nationalism, not narrow provincialism, but a magnificent economic union of the whole world.
I wonder if the hon. member for Maple Creek was quite in earnest when he made 1-hat statement. I am sure he is a close student of economics and of the tariff, and I fail to see personally where this trend towards internationalism is taking place, so far as the tariff is concerned. In the matter of freer trade, of which he speaks, when we look to England we find the Safeguarding of Industries Act. If we look to the example of our neighbours to the south and study the Fordnev-McCumber tariff which was enacted there, or if we refer to the German tariff, or to the tariff brought into force in any other country in the world since the conclusion of the war, we will find that all these countries -including England in the matter of her Safeguarding of Industries Act-are increasing

The Budget-Mr. Jacobs
their tariff. Therefore I hope the hon. member for Maple Creek will do us the favour of showing at another time where this trend of internationalism or freer trade is taking place.
Speaking of the visit of the Saskatchewan members to the Dominion Textile plants at Montreal, I only hope that these gentlemen, coming as they do from the west, have been enlightened as to the true industrial situation. I trust that as Canadians, looking over those plants and seeing the number of men employed, they realized then, if they had not realized before, that in the interests of our industrial life the manufacturers of this country must be protected. I was rather nonplussed at the attitude of the hon. member for Maple Creek. I was surprised that after seeing what the industrial life of Canada meant he should come back and immediately upon taking his seat start on the rampage with respect to free trade and this movement towards internationalism which he says is taking place, but which is not taking place; free trade, he knows, is a myth. I trust that these Liberal members not only visited the factories and saw the industrial life there, but that they also took occasion to visit some of the men who were not at their places in the factories but were out of employment. I hope they felt in their visits to those homes that these men are patrons of Canadian industry and Canadians at heart even as the hon. gentlemen themselves are. I hope that the hon. gentlemen will also bear in mind that even if the farmers of the west have had hard times at intervals, there are times in the industrial life of our cities, especially when men are out of work and cannot get employment in the factories, that we look for some consideration in the matter of a protective tariff, and that they will see their way clear to cooperate with us and not be so scared, as they seemingly appear to be on that side of the House, of the word "protection." There is nothing to justify the view that there is anything to be afraid of in that connection.

I believe these are the only remarks I have to make with reference to the budget, and I have only this to say in closing. Many comments have emanated from this side <of the House with respect to the hon. Minister of Immigration (Mr. Forke). If there is one member of the government who carries a burden on his shoulders and upon whom I should like to pin the rose of hope, it is the Minister of Immigration. I sincerely trust that in the exercise of his duties and the discharge of the responsibility that rests upon him he will do his share in bringing to this country a great number of immigrants who will find in Canada a country worth while and who will remain here. I hope the minister will be able to stop the migration out of this country which has been so often debated here and which I will not weary the House by referring to at the present time. I think if one minister in the government deserves some consideration and some praise, dr it may be, help from the opposition, we should at least give that minister the preference. In closing may I express the wish that he will be able to show us in the near future that he is meeting success in his arduous duties and accomplishing all that the situation demands.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the observations which I have to offer to the House this evening will be of the briefest kind. The country is waiting for the vote which will decide the fate of this government, and I do not want to keep it in suspense a moment longer than I can help. In order to relieve their minds, my remarks will be noted for their brevity if for nothing else.
The hon. member for Macleod (Mr. Coote) introduced an amendment to the budget which if carried will mean the defeat of the Liberal party. I wonder if the hon. member when he drafted his motion thought what that would mean for the party to which he belonged. Does he not believe like every sensible man that "half a loaf is better than no bread?" We are standing between him and this awful, wicked Conservative party. He does not give us credit for that. I wonder if he has read the history of Charles II? When the king's brother, the Duke of York, counselled His Majesty not to expose himself so freely on the street as it might entail his assassination, Charles II, who was a very wise and very witty monarch replied:	The
people of England are too sensible to murder me in order to put you in my place.
The Budget-Mr. Jacobs

The amendment of the hon. gentleman is what is known technically as "eye-wash." It is not to be taken seriously, yet here it is and we have to deal with it. But within the next few minutes we shall be all out of our troubles when the vote is taken.
'The hon. leader of the opposition to-day delivered a most eloquent and instructive address. It, was noted for its eloquence, for his abnegation of Liberal principles, and was in effect a bid for the leadership of the Tory party of which he is now one of the shining ornaments. Within the last few days we have had the spectacle in parliament of three or four aspirants to the leadership of the Tory party, standing up, saying what they had to say eloquently, and well, and leaving it to, their party to indicate who is to be selected. It reminded me of the judgment of Paris. There were three ladies who presented themselves to Paris. He examined them as to their beauty-and there was a great deal to be seen-and after he had given his decision in favour of one-because there was only one to be selected, provoked the great Trojan war, and you know1 the catastrophe that happened after that. Well, I hone no such event will happen after the leader of the Tory party has been permanently named. I admire the leader of the opposition. I remember when I heard him first on May 29, 1912, in the city of Montreal. The bloom of youth was then on his cheek, and I remember well the florid complexion of the young man who sat close to the great chief of the Liberal party. He thundered in tones so eloquent against the Tories that I thought to myself: "Me-thinks the lady doth protest too much." I could not at that time believe that he was making a bid for the vacancy which has been occasioned on the other side by the retirement of Mr. Meighen.
We spoke yesterday in this House about the exportable surplus of wheat. We have an exportable surplus of Liberalism. We have so much of that commodity on this side of the House that our cup of joy is overflowing and we are willing to divide it with our friends on the other side. Some wit in this House remarked last fall after the election and after the appointment of the leader of the opposition to his present position:	"Well,
this is a great year for the Liberal party. We have a Liberal Prime Minister; we have a Liberal leader of the opposition, and we have a Liberal leader oif the Progressive party. Everything seems to !be coming our way." How true is the saying of the Psalmist:
The stone which the builders rejected, the same is become the head of the corner.

The hon. gentleman is a great lawyer. He would have made his mark had he remained at the bar. After listening to his eloquence to-day and after comparing it with his eloquence before 1917, I can see what a great lawyer he is. He talks on both sides with equal facility, I wish the time would come when I could do likewise. Perhaps if a vacancy on the other side occurred, I might-
. An hon. MEMBER:	Consider it.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
-consider it. He argued
to-day that there is no surplus; that it is all camouflage; that it does not exist. Notwithstanding the fact that there is no surplus, the Minister of Finance is in a position to cut down the sales tax by 20 per cent, to cut down the income tax, to make a substantial reduction in the national debt and so on, all, mark you, without any surplus. I ask myself: If the Minister of Finance is able to do that, what could he really do if he had a surplus? He is a miracle worker and as such we want him. Moses struck the rock and produced water. It flowed freely. Moses is not a patch or circumstance on the present Minister of Finance who is able to do these wonderful things.
Altogether I think the Conservative party is very fortunate in having a man of the ability of the leader of the opposition. He talks intelligently, cogently, with lucidity, and he has tasted of the tree of knowledge and of good and evil-he knows both sides. The old saying is true:
And still they gazed, and still the wonder
grew,
That one small head should carry all he knew.
I wonder where all these apologies of Conservatism, all these high-minded utterances which we heard to-day respecting the Tory party and its glories, were hidden during the years from 1900 to 1917 when the hon. gentleman was one of the ornaments of this side of the House. He disguised them very well, but I am glad now that he has scope for his abilities and I hope the Tory party will keep on with the hon. gentleman as its head.
We had some discussion in this House a little while ago about the appointment to Washington. The appointment has at last been made and the Hon. Mr. Massey is the first minister from Canada accredited to any country. I think this country is to be congratulated on the appointment of Mr. Massey to that high and honourable position. Mr. Massey fits the position admirably. He is a man of education, of culture, with the neces^ sary resources to keep up a position of that

The Budget-Mr. Jacobs
kind, and he is bound to make good. It is only right that we should have a representative at Washington. After all $1,000,000,000 or one-half of the entire trade of this country is with the United States. We have 115,000,000 people on one side of the border and
10,000,000 people on the other side, with tens of thousands of people crossing this border every day. Every possible kind of trade is transacted daily between the two countries. We have questions to diiscuss as regards railway bonding privileges, smuggling, narcotic drug traffic, white slave traffic, and matters of all kinds, which are of the highest importance, and the surprise to me is that we have remained so long without a representative at Washington.
There are many things that the Hon. Mr. Massey can do while he is at Washington. For instance, he can point out to the authorities there that we resent the discrimination that exists with regard to Canadian citizens who go to the United States. As hon. members know, the United States divides the Canadian people into two classes; those who were born in Canada and those who came to Canada from foreign parts. Those who were bom in Canada can go freely into the United States either to visit or to reside permanently. Those who were born outside of this Dominion are permitted to enter the United States only on what is known as the two per cent quota of the country of their origin. What has been the result? Within the first six months of last year 50,000 Canadian citizens crossed the border by the highroad. I have not the figures for the last six months, but I fancy that an equal number left here for that country. Therefore we have 100,000 Canadian-born citizens who went to the United States within one year. I know what hon. gentlemen on the other side are thinking, namely, that if we had a high protective tariff, they would not have gone. But that is not the point I wish to make. The point I wish to make is that the United States of America is discriminating between native-born citizens and foreign-born citizens of this country, both British subjects, mark you. They take the certificate of naturalization of a foreign-bom citizen who wishes to enter their country and pay no attention to it; they treat it as a scrap of paper. They discriminate. We do not. After all, when we give a certificate of naturalization to a foreign-bom- after he has remained here for a certain period, after he has behaved himself like a respectable citizen, he is treated by us in the same way as if he were bom in this country. But when he goes to the United States bc-undary, they, forsooth, would
make a distinction. Why is that? I will tell the House why it is. The United States for some time have put into force this immigration quota because they want in that country people coming from what they call the Nordic portions of Europe. They do not want anybody except the Nordics. The basis of the population in Canada is Nordic. Consequently they insist upon having what they -call the best element in this .community 

the -Canadian-born, the man who understands American conditions, and who does not require to become Americanized, and so on. They are draining this country of the best element we have, and -are leaving us the foreign^born. Mark you, I am mot making any objection to the foreign-bom. We welcome them -and are glad to have them, -but, everything -being equal, I think it will be admitted -by everyone here that the Canadian born citizen is perhaps the better for this country than the fo-reign-bom. He is not obliged to unlearn anything and -adjust -himself to -a different environment.
Why is it that so many of our people are going to the United States? The -reason is this:	That under -their -quota law, they take
in between 100,000 and 150,000 immigrants every year, and n-o more. Before this quota law went into effect, they were taking in f-rom
1,000,000 to 1,500,000. How are they going to make good the wastage in their -country? By draining off our native-born Canadian citizens, -bringing them to the United States and absorbing them with their own people. I ask you, M-r. Speaker, is it right -that -we should stand by and see a -thing of that kind done without making some protest .to -the American -government? Is it -right? I do not think it is. When we give a person a certificate of naturalization, we have to protect him in every way -possible in which a government can protect its people, but as soon as he begins to use his certificate of naturalization, he is told that it is of no use to him at all in the United States.
The United States claim to be a country of freedom, of liberty, and so on. In -the year 1910 discrimination was made by -the empire of Russi-a against American citizens entering that country. Russia declared that people of a certain religious persuasion could not enter the empire of Russia although -they were American citizens; I have reference to Jewish people. There were only two classes who were allowed to enter. They had either to -be bankers-I -ask my friends -of the Progressive movement to listen to that-or they had to be people of high social standing.
The Budget-Mr. Jacobs

After all, all the people of the limited States who travel are not bankers or people of high social standing, and it was the Russian police who had to decide whether they were bankers or people of high social standing. If the American citizen desiring to enter Russia handed over a sum which was sufficient to indicate that he was a banker, he entered freely, and no doubt the same was true with regard to people of high social standing. President Taft took this matter up with Russia. There was a treaty between these countries which was entered into in 1832, and representations were made to the Russian government, through the American ambassador in St. Petersburg. The Russian government was then tottering to its fall, and no action was taken. The treaty was denounced, and since 1910 there has been no treaty between Russia and the United States, because they felt, and rightly so, that no such discrimination should be made against United States citizens. When a United States citizen presented his certificate he was able to say "Civis Americanus sum", and that was sufficient- To-day the United States are practising the same thing which Russia practised up to 1910, and it seems to me the part of wisdom for ouir government, through our minister, to point out to the American government that they are not giving us a square deal. If they want our people, we cannot hold them back, but at least we ought to ask the American government to take What is known in Nova Scotia as rum-of-mine.
I suppose a good many members of the Progressive party are unaware of the fact that they could not enter the United States except under the quota law. My good friend from Red Deer (Mr. Speakman), the member for Peace River (Mr. Kennedy), the member for Bow River (Mr. Garland), and the members for other creeks and rivers-I cannot remember them all-would not be permitted, not one O'f them, to enter the United States except under the quota law, and in some cases they would have to wait ten years, and in other cases fifteen, before they could get in. So what can these poor people do? They have to run for parliament and !be elected to this House.
Although we have not got a quota law in this country, we have something which is so near unto it that it would take a Philadelphia lawyer to decide what the difference is. We do not put a quota law into effect, but we have drawn a line across the map of Europe and we say: These people from the northern part may come in, but these people from the south and

southeastern part shall not come in. I do not suppose that it is generally known-I do not think the Minister of Immigration is aware that he is keeping out the entire Latin race from entering this country, with the exception of the French. Naturally they could not keep the French out, because they would hear about it in this House. The French are permitted to come in, but no other members of the Latin race, except under special permit and privilege. Now that is- a rather serious thing. After all, there are decent people among the Latin race who make good citizens. The test of a man's ability to make good in this country is not the country fr6m which he comes; it is the character of the man. The whole of southeastern Europe is in what is known as the non-preferred class. Asia Minor is in the non-preferred class.
I am going to say' something which will probably surprise my friend the Minister of Immigration, and that is that under the rules of the Immigration department the founder of Christianity would be debarred from coming into this country. He could not come in, and none of the apostles could enter this country. None of the founders of the early Christian church could enter Canada under the present regulations of the department. There are in the case of Jesus of Nazareth,-I am saying it with all respect-four orders in council which would prohibit him from coming in here. There would be first, the order relating to the non-agriculturist class. Carpenters are not permitted to enter this country coming from that district. And then he would not have a proper passport; he wrould not be travelling by a continuous journey; and he would have no relatives in this country. Those are four orders in council which would prevent him from coming in. Michael Angelo, although he built St. Peter's at Rome, could not enter this country, because we do not want architects or carpenters from Latin countries. If he came from Iceland and could build an icehouse, we could use him. If Mr. Mussolini wished to come over and make a bid for the leadership of the Tory party, he would be debarred by the Minister of Immigration from coming in. We heard it stated in the last election: Canada wants a Mussolini. But my friend the Minister of Immigration stands like an angel with flaming sword at the gate, and would not permit him to enter. And so all along the line.
It seems to me, Mr. Speaker, that this country is not in a position now to make distinctions between people as to the countries

from which they come. A man may be a scoundrel and come from Scandinavia; a man may be a genius and come from Italy. I have dinned this thing into the ears of the Department of Immigration for the last ten years.
I have been a voice crying in the wilderness.
I have not been able to make them see the light. My friend the Minister of Immigration made some very interesting and satisfactory speeches before he came down here to take the department in hand. In Winnipeg I remember he made a speech which made us believe that at last there was a Daniel come to judgment; he was going to do wonderful things. He pointed out that hitherto the department, unfortunately, had had so many temporary ministers and so many ministers who had not had time to get acquainted with conditions before they moved on that they were unable to do justice to themselves and to the department. He was going to do it justice. Well I hope he will. He is a new man and certainly is not lacking in intelligence and has many qualities which go to make a splendid administrator, and I hope that when he takes hold of things, all this red tape which seems to embarrass the immigration department will be cut away and flung into the waste paper basket. It will be a good thing for the department, a good thing for the minister and, best of all, it will be a good thing for the country.
May I say a word or two about the question of the maritime rights which will be before the House very shortly? It would appear that the maritimes have rights. I have not read the report yet, but I have no doubt they have rights. A commission was appointed by the government to investigate and ascertain what those rights were and are. The commission sat during last summer and the early part of the autumn. They made their final report. A curious thing about the commission, which I think should be brought to the attention of the House, is the fact that although the commission consisted of three worthy members, men who are looked upon as of first class ability in their respective avocations, no counsel was appointed to represent the Dominion government. Do hon. members not think that an extraordinary thing? Here were gentlemen from the maritimes who were interested in seeing that adjustments were made of conditions in the maritimes which they thought had been brought about by forces over which they had no control. They were making claims for tens of millions of dollars. They were to have adjustment of freight rates, and they
The Budget-Mr. Jacobs
were to have coking plants to stimulate the coal business in Nova Scotia, and dozens of other things which involved large expenditures on the part of the Dominion government. Can hon. members tell me why no person was there to represent the government, to cross-examine them and find out the basis of their claims? In the customs inquiry, which is being conducted so efficiently, we find two legal gentlemen who are drawing, in addition to their breath, $300 a day from the coffers of this country. There never was a commission in which the party who is going to have money extracted from him is not represented in some way. After all, there must be some person to see that they do not walk away with the parliament buildings. And yet the fact remains that in this case nothing was done. The report was prepared and handed in without any examination at all of the witnesses by the federal authorities. The reason of it was, I think, that when the commission began its1 sittings we were in the throes of a general election. Both parties-and I may say the three parties-were so busy saving their own political lives that they had not time to consider the way in which this thing was being conducted, and the result is the maritimes walked away with practically everything they asked. I think that when the case comes before the House we should bear in mind that this was what is known as an ex parte judgment. The Dominion government was not represented, and we should scrutinize very carefully indeed any sums of money we pay in a case where we are not represented. In Quebec certain proceedings are taken in cases where the party is not represented. We make an opposition to judgment. We take out a petition in revocation of judgment. We say we have not been justly treated, and the case is thereupon opened upon the necessary affidavit being made, and the party who complains has an opportunity of placing his case before the court. I cannot absolve the Meighen government from responsibility in this matter. After all, the commission functioned at the time the Meighen government _ was functioning. They were both functioning concurrently. Surely there must have been in the Tory party, who had been out of office for such a long period of time, some lawyer who could take up the brief for the Dominion government, and yet nothing was done. We are now faced with a situation of that kind, and I think the people of this country will demand some accountability from the parties responsible for what I would call a denial of justice.
The Budget-Mr. Jacobs

With regard to the suggestion made by the hon. member for West Calgary (Mr. Bennett) I say that to my mind it was the most constructive suggestion that has been made in the House this session. It seeks to reduce the interest charges on our public debt; and with a sinking fund, it seeks also eventually to abolish our debt altogether. Of course that will not come in my day or in the day of any gentleman listening to the sound of my voice to-night. But it seems to me to be a step in the proper direction, and it would be Well if this suggestion were sent to the banking and commerce committee and thrown to the young lions of the Progressive party so that we could see what they would make of it. It is something well worth considering, and the fact that it is not taken very seriously by the banking community of this country is proof to my mind that it is a pretty good thing. I think the bankers can be induced to see that it is in their interest to have something of that kind done. It is proposed to let them have four per cent upon their money, and as the hon. member for West Calgary said they have hundreds of millions lying idle, in some cases bearing not more than two or two and a half per cent, when they are helping the government they are helping themselves, because after all they are the largest taxpayers in the country. They are the people who will benefit first when we get our finances on an even keel, and I think it is only necessary for us to charge the hon. member for West Calgary, not professionally of course but what is known as amicus curise, to go down and visit his friends in the Sodom and Gomorrah of unrighteousness in Toronto and Montreal, pointing out to them the feasibility of the project and that it would enure as much to their benefit as to the people at large; something tangible would come of it.
I am always very wary of suggestions from my friends on the other side. Beware of the Greeks bringing gifts. Something good may come out of Nazareth, and the hon. member for West Calgary is too big a man to put forward something of this ldnd as a cat's paw, and I know he would be able to convince other people that the scheme is workable and would bring to the country tens of millions of dollars ' in due course.
I have no feeling that the government is going to be defeated. I do not think they will be, but if they are we will meet again at Philippi. We have trounced the Tory party successively three times now, and I think we are able to do it a fourth. At any rate, we are willing to try and let the best man win. I think the Minister of Finance 
ought to be congratulated upon this splendid budget of his. I think he deserves a great deal of credit for the brevity of the budget speech. In the olden days budget speeches used to take three and four hours and one could not understand what was being said because of the abundance of words. This is a business man's speech delivered by a business man in thirty-five minutes, a speech which everybody could understand and which raised the parliament of Canada in the estimation of the whole country. I only hope that we shall have the present Minister (Mr. Robb) for many years to direct the finances of the country. I support the main motion.
M:r. R. K. SMITH (Cumberland): It is not my intention to unduly delay the House this evening. I did not intend making any reference to the Duncan report at this time, but after listening to the hon. gentleman who has just concluded (Mr. Jacobs) I am bound to say that we are surprised to learn that any hon. member of this House could have been tempted to treat that subject in the humorous manner in which that hon. member has. The order in council creating the Duncan commission was passed last year when the present Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) was m office, and the instructions conveyed in the right hon. gentleman's letter to the commission were given during the month of April last. I understand that my hon. friend who has just sat down is a man of outstanding ability, learned in the law, and I should think that the Prime Minister, if he wanted to appoint counsel to assist the commission, could not have made any better choice than the hon. gentleman himself. But there was no necessity for counsel in connection with that investigation for the reason that there was not involved any question of law of a technical character such as would warrant the employment of a legal man. The matter for investigation had reference to certain unfair conditions there, and the object was to ascertain what remedies could be applied to alleviate those conditions, which have existed in the maritime provinces ever since confederation. I trust that the .party opposite will not generally treat the subject as humourously as my hon. friend has.

speechtext: In what sense did I treat the report humorously? I pointed out that there was no counsel, and that is no laughing matter.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I listened carefully to the hon. gentleman's whole speech, which was full of a delicate humour at the expense of the report, and the tone he adopted

The Budget-Mr. Smith (Cumberland)
in relation to the investigation is in keeping with the rest of his remarks. His reference to the fact that no counsel had been appointed was presumably ironical; it was altogether unnecessary.
I want to put myself on record as being disappointed, as all of us from eastern Canada are bitterly disappointed, and indeed properly perturbed, that the budget contains no relief for the two basic industries of Nova Scotia. We are particularly disconcerted at this, in view of the information which we gave this House and the present Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) during the last session of parliament. If our words, our pleas and our testimony have no weight with the minister, if he is inclined to be sceptical of the seriousness of the situation and if he takes this position because of the policy of ' the party to which he belongs, surely there is reason for him to have some regard not only for the pleas of the .people generally, and of all political parties in Nova Scotia, but also for the recommendations of the royal commissions appointed by this government and by the province as well. The royal commission appointed by Nova Scotia in 1925, in an addendum, to its report, suggested an increased duty on coal and steel, and the royal commission appointed last year by this very government also recommended, at least by implication, further protection on coal. Let me read from the Duncan report the paragraph regarding the customs tariff on coal.
Several phases of the customs tariff in its relation to coal were brought to our attention both by the government of Nova Scotia and by the operators of the coal mines. These we feel ourselves precluded from dealing with since they are a matter properly to be considered by the Tariff Advisory Board, but we may be permitted to say that we are impressed with the need for reconsideration of the customs tariff in its relation to coal and anthracite coke and recommend that the Tariff Advisory Board should be asked to give immediate consideration to the subject.
Let me stress some words of that paragraph: "We are impressed with the need for reconsideration of the customs tariff in its relation to coal." There can be no reconsideration of the customs tariff on coal in a downward direction; such reconsideration must have an upward trend. Still, notwithstanding the fact that an application was presented to the government in 1924 by a delegation 'headed by the then Premier of Nova Scotia, Mr. Armstrong, asking for increased protection on coal; notwithstanding that in an addendum to its report the royal commission appointed by the government of Nova Scotia in 1925 recommended the same thing; and notwithstanding
that the royal commission appointed by this government itself now urges a higher protection in this direction, we 'have in the year 1927 a budget brought down by the Minister of Finance in which this important industry and all the recommendations are totally ignored.

speechtext: How will increased protection on coal improve the steel industry in Canada?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The steel industry is linked up with the coal industry, particularly in eastern Canada, to such an extent that it is almost impossible to separate the two. We have information to the effect that in Nova Scotia-and this applies to the rest of Canada-it takes four tons of coal to produce a ton of steel, so that whatever you do for the benefit of coal will assist steel, and vice versa.

speechtext:
That is quite a different construction ^rom the one placed on those words by the hon. member for Kings-Hants (Mr. Ilsley). I was going to say, Mr. Speaker, that possibly the Minister of Finance might say that this is properly a question for reference to the Tariff Advisory Board, and in connection with that board let me say a few words. I know nothing of its personnel but I do know that it has no power; in my opinion it has not even enough power to be self-respecting. There is a saying which I used in the House last year which seems to me particularly applicable to this board; it has powder in its canister but no shot in its locker. It has no power to make a finding, can only make a recommendation, and it appears to me to be a vehicle for the shelving
780	COMMONS
The Budget-Mr. Smith (Cumberland)
of troublesome questions when they are such. Last year, however, after the Tariff Advisory Board was constituted, a tariff matter was absolutely taken out of its hands in connection with the reduction of duty on automobiles. If this board is to be something worth while is it the policy of the government to place before it questions of a troublesome nature in order to escape responsiblity, and on the other hand to take any political advantage possible through a popular reduction in the tariff by using their own judgment without referring the matter to the board at all?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Was the tariff board inaugurated at the- time the automobile duty was removed?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The tariff
board was properly constituted before the duty on automobiles was dealt with last year, and I do not believe that to be a fair proposal to the industries of this country. If the board is to be made something worth while and something which will function properly, certainly it must be used in a proper way and not as a means of sidetracking troublesome questions. It should be used to secure all the information available and forward it in their findings to this House.
The question has arisen, Mr. Speaker, as to whether or not the coal industry in Canada is worth while. Last year in Nova Scotia we produced 6,300,000 tons of coal, slightly more than in the year previous; one-fifth of the population of that province is directly dependent upon the coal and steel industries and one-twelfth of the revenue of Nova Scotia is secured from royalities on coal. In the Dominion of Canada we have invested about $150,000,000 in coal mining, and1 the coal business in Canada has attained a value of as high as $80,000,000 in one year. I say, Mr. Speaker, that it is an industry which we must protect. If the coal industry in Nova Scotia is allowed to go by the board and disappear, there will also disappear from the province of Nova Scotia one-fifth of its population and one-twelfth of its revenue, and chaos will be created in the business of that province. But someone will say that there is no danger of the coal industry in Canada disappearing; I say there is a very grave danger unless something is done to properly protect it. Last year we imported from the United States about 17,000,000 tons of coal, of which 13,000,000 tons were of the very grade we produce in Nova Scotia. It has been said that some day anthracite coal in the United States will be exhausted, and when that time comes we must look elsewhere for our hard coal, or for 
a substitute. We should be independent of the United States with regard to bituminous coal as well as anthracite, because we do not know when we may be cut off from this supply. A war, a strike, or any other contingency may at any time stop the importation of American coal into Canada, and we have no way of looking ahead and guarding against these things, except by developing our own industries. We should be prepared to meet such conditions, and that can only be done by becoming independent of that country in relation to coal.
On the Canadian National railways last year we used 5,000,000 tons of coal, 3,000,000 tons of which came from the United States. It does not seem to me that we are treating our coal industry fairly; it certainly deserves something better than that. We are not asking for high protection, as some hon. gentlemen opposite would like to make people believe; we are asking for a moderate, adequate protection, something that should be granted readily because the duty to-day is practically the same as it was in the eighties while the protection is less than half as much, for obvious reasons which need no elaboration. We are asking for an adequate duty to protect this industry, and as soon as it is found that proper protection is given, the duty if need be may be very readily lessened. Some may say that this will have a tendency to increase the price of coal in Canada; in that connection I have here some of the remarks of Mr. Cronyn, which are very pertinent, but with which I will not weary the House. It does seem to me, however, that if the output of coal could be doubled in Canada there would be an appreciable difference in the cost of production, more than enough, I believe, to offset the increased duty. I believe that duty should be $1 per ton, and I believe if that duty is granted, with the coking plants which we hope to see established and with the freight reductions which are promised, we can establish an all-Canadian coal supply for an all-Canadian market.
