Now, Mr. Speaker, I am going to leave the question of coal and speak about two other industries in the province of Nova Scotia that are Very severely affected by the customs tariff. Last year I brought to the
1, 1927	781
The Budget-Mr. Smith (Cumberland)
attention of the House and of the Minister of Finance a languishing shoe industry which happens to be located in the town from which I come. That shoe industry was languishing last year. This year it is dead. It has gone into liquidation and is now in the hands of a receiver, due to unfair competition coming mostly from the old country. That industry was established away back in the year 1867. It has progressed almost^ every year down until about 1921. But to-day it is in the hands of a receiver. Why we should allow unfair competition to interfere with any legitimate industry in this country is more than I can understand. The Prime Minister has made the statement in this House and out of it, that no legitimate industry in Canada would suffer through his fiscal policy. This industry is certainly legitimate and it is surely suffering from the policy of inadequate protection. This applies not only to the shoe industry in the. province from which I come but to the industry all over the Dominion to a very marked degree. Why, Mr. Speaker, the boot and shoe manufacturers have to pay from fifteen to thirty-five per cent duty on the raw material that goes into the manufacture of some of our boots and shoes in this country, whereas in the old country, they get their raw material free. Last year there were imported into the Dominion 809,483 pairs of shoes to the value of two million odd dollars. We exported from Canada during the same period -these are figures for the year ending January, 1927-110,337 pairs. I have a lot of figures here but I am not going to weary the House with them. It is sufficient to note that we are steadily increasing the importations of boots and shoes,-and leather goods manufactured and unmanufactured, into the Dominion. It certainly is not a healthy sign. It shows very positively that there is something radically wrong with the tariff and its application to this business, and the government at least should recognize the fact that it requires a little more consideration and a higher degree of protection.
I spoke also last year with regard to the woollen industry. We have a woollen mill in the' town whence I come which is boarded up, due to unfair competition from abroad. The textiles and fibres which were imported into this country during the year ending January, 1927, amounted to a little uader $200,000,000-1184,000,000 odd. We imported in 1926, $181,000,000 odd, and in 1925, $163,000,000 odd, showing a steady increase in the importations of textiles and fibres into Canada. Look at our exports. During the same period of

The Budget-Mr. Smith (Cumberland)
1925 when we imported $163,000,000 odd, we exported nine millions odd. In 1928 we exported but nine millions odd, and in 1927, a lesser amount of seven million dollars odd. We imported from the United Kingdom last year to the extent of $72,000,000 odd, but we exported to that country only $844,000 odd. These figures are for the year ending January, 1927. We imported from the United States $69,000,000 odd, and exported to that country $3,000,000 odd. I think these figures speak in no uncertain tones as to the position of the textile industry in this country and what it requires. It has been said in this chamber that Penman's are doing much more business than they did previously, that their bonds are high. Penman's may be progressing, but the smaller mills in the Dominion are the ones that are suffering. The smaller mills all over the Dominion are unable to meet that unfair competition; they are unable to compete with the wage rate, lower to the extent of one-half, that is paid in the old land, and with other unfair conditions. They certainly cannot meet that competition on anything like a fair basis unless some further tariff protection is granted.
I am going to conclude by stating that in the maritimes to-day there is one matter transcending all others in importance, and that is the implementing by legislation by this government of all the recommendations contained in the Duncan report. We have passed the stage of trifling in connection with this matter. We will discuss the issues dealt with in the report later. It will not be amiss, however, for me to state now that all the people of the maritime provinces are of one mind on this report, namely, that it should be speedily implemented in toto by legislation by this parliament.at this session. Anything short of that-any delay, amendment or mutilation-will meet with such hostility from eastern Canada that I hesitate to mention in this House what sort of revolution will take place.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
We
have listened, Mr. Speaker, during this debate to a great flow of oratory, and a great many figures which would lead to the conclusion that one could prove almost, anything from figures. Some of the arguments which I have heard do not seem to be very sound-in fact there were a number which appeared to me to be very absurd.
I take the Hansard of yesterday and I find in the remarks of the hon. member for Frontenac-Addington (Mr. Edlwardb) as reported on two pages not very far apart, an argument in one place that the imposition of a duty increases the price of wheat, and in

another that the effect of the imposition of a duty is not to raise the price of a protected article. On page 736 of Hansard the hon. member is reported as saying:
The purpose of protection is not to raise prices but to defend and develop the purchasing power of the nation.	,
Those are very plain words. On the next page the hon. member for Moose Jaw made this statement:
Mr. Ross (Moose Jaw) : The hon. gentleman will admit that a duty of 42 cents a bushel on wheat does not raise the price of wheat in the United States for the simple reason that they have an exportable surplus.
The hon. member for Frontenac-Addington proceeded to demonstrate that in the United States they have a duty on wheat, a duty,on eggs, and a duty on butter, and he asked: Are the legislators of the United States all deceived? No other conclusion can be drawn from that than that he believes and they believe that the imposition of a duty raises the price of those goods in the United States. Thus we find contradictory remarks on two pages, one immediately following the other. The hon. member for Frontenac-Addington is entirely wrong in regard to wheat. He stated that if the imposition of a duty on manufactured goods raises the price, it must follow that the imposition of a duty on wheat in Canadb. raises the price, because he said, as we have a duty of 12 cents a bushel on wheat -I think he is wrong in that; I think the duty is 8 cents a bushel-the farmers must have reaped, because of that duty, a profit of $10,000,000.
This is what really takes place. He made the statement-and on the other side of the House a goodly number of members applauded it-that if it were true that the imposition of a protective duty raised the price of manufactured articles, it would also have the same effect on wheat. Why does it not? On the surface it seems rational that it should. This is the reason: The price of our Wheat is fixed in the old country market. You have to bring your competition to bear on the governing market and our governing market for wheat is in the old country. I think the hon. member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Ross) was partly right and partly wrong when he stated that the duty placed by the United States government on Canadian and other wheat going into that country did not raise the price of the wheat in the United States. In the United States they have an area that grows strong, hard wheat, of which they have not sufficient, of which they are very short. The imposition of a duty against Canadian wheat does protect that wheat and does raise the

The Budget-Mr. Millar
price of it. On the other hand they have also large areas that grow soft wheat of which they have a surplus. That wheat is not greatly in demand. They require perhaps more of it than they do of hard wheat; but still they do not require all of it, and they export part of it. Thus we have an example in the one country, the United States, of a protective tariff raising the price of a part of a commodity and not affecting the other part. The governing market for the soft wheat is the old country, the same as is the case with us. The governing market for the hard wheat is in their own country, and that is where you can protect and where you can raise the price. But you cannot do that with Canadian wheat. Our price is governed by the price in Liverpool.
The hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens), who is not in his seat at present, and a few other hon. members have directed some attention to the group that sit in this row of benches where I sit, and I wish to make some comment upon their remarks. If one is charged in a court of justice one wants to know what the charge is and what is the proof of his guilt. There were others in this row who were elected on an arrangement somewhat similar to the one on which I was elected. I was elected as a Liberal-Progressive, and I wonder if the charge is made because I have joined up with another group that has a very similar platform. I would not mind being accused of that. In fact if I were to be charged with anything of that nature, joining another party, crossing the floor to or linking up in any way with another party, I would suggest to the hon. member for Vancouver Centre that two of the judges might be the leader of the opposition (Mr. Guthrie) and the hon. member for Fort William (Mr. Manion). Perhaps they would know as much about how it felt whether or not they were apostates, whether they were criminals, whether they deserved to be treated as the Minister of Immigration (Mr. Forke) has been treated. Some have laughed because the Liberal-Progressives have taken their seats on this side of the House.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
An hon. member says:
" hear, hear." To go back at little, let me ask: Is there any disgrace in being elected as a Progressive with Liberal support or as a Conservative with Progressive support? I do not think there is any reason whjr I should be ashamed when two groups in my constituency, whose views on the tariff and on other matters are almost identical, agreed to come
together and to choose a candidate as they did, and I was elected. And when I come to this House, where is the logical place for me to sit?' There are only two: one with the Progressives, and the other on this side of the House. I do not think there is any blame whatever attaching to me, no matter which I choose; I could be damned for doing either. Is there any good reason why the hon. member for Vancouver Centre, who perhaps has been dealing a little to much in mud of late and has become too handy at throwing it, should point to this group and say we have betrayed our principles? While his attention was directed chiefly towards the Minister of Immigration, it certainly must have included others as well. Is there any reason to believe that we are not doing our best to get what we consider to be in the interests of the country? Is there any reason to believe that we uphold evil? Is there any reason to believe that we are not as true as when we were elected in 1921? I do not think so.
The farmers' platfonn spoken of by the hon. member for Vancouver Centre was drawn up about 1912 and I believe it was revised in 1917. The hon. member for Vancouver Centre read over this platform and, referring then to the Minister of Immigration, he used the word " apostate ", stating that there were those who had betrayed the people who trusted' them. I would point out that many changes have taken place since then. We have had many reductions in the tariff. There have been very many changes that would cause one to take a different view. Besides, since I have been here I have not been standing still. I do not think one is necessarily to blame if he should change his views as he listens to arguments, comes into contact with other members, and hears them discuss their problems. If there is any member on the other side of the House who has not changed his mind in five years, I would like to see him stand up. The implication of the hon. member for Vancouver Centre was that because one did not act exactly as he did when that platform was drawn up, he was an apostate and a traitor. Well, if there is any member on the other side of the House who has not changed his mind in five years, though he may think he liveth, I think he is dead,
I am going to direct my attention now to some measures that it seems to me might help to improve the condition of Canada. I am inclined to think that perhaps too much attention has been paid to the tariff question. It is good fighting ground, and I suppose that is
The Budget-Mr. Millar

the reason why it is discussed at great length every session. But the tariff question is not all. I freely say that I am not entirely satisfied with the present budget so far as the tariff is concerned. I was elected, 'as many other hon. members were, on a low tariff platform, and I hope tQ get that low tariff as quickly as possible. I believe in a low tariff, but since listening to the remarks of other members I confess that I have changed my mind slightly in some particulars, though on the whole I am of the same opinion regarding the tariff as I was when I came here in 1921. We have had. changes made in the tariff since 1921, some in 1924, but I would like to see the Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) go a little further.
I might have had reason to vote against the budget if it were not for the fact that we have had a tariff board appointed. I thought this matter over very fully. Last session was a very hectic one, and it was followed immediately by an election. Then came the conference of the premiers in London. I know that private members are very, very busy, and ministers are much more so, and I cannot see how it would be possible for the government to have the time necessary to weigh carefully all the data gathered by the tariff board in the short time that elapsed before the opening of the session. You know what it means to peruse the evidence taken down by a shorthand writer covering the proceedings of only one day. To sift that evidence and study it in relation to other matters is no small task, and I do not think any member who desired to be fair would say that it was possible for the government to consider that data properly and bring down any important tariff changes based upon it at this session. I have no hesitation in saying, however, that when next session rolls around I shall expect, if I am here, very radical changes in the tariff. I hope there will be reductions all along the line, but for the present I cannot severely criticise the government for not doing that which I feel it was physically impossible for them to do.	,*
The hon. member for Toronto West Centre (Mr. Hocken) referred to the income tax, as he does almost every session, and he pointed out that the farmers are paying very little income tax. I have been struck more than once with the nerve of those who, after they have grasped what belongs to themselves and three or four others will then stand back and pour ridicule and scorn on those who have not paid the income tax. If I have my share of the goods of this world and the share of
(Mr. Millar.]	.
three or four others as well, I have no right to ridicule the others if they do not pay their share of the income tax, and that is exactly what has taken place. The farmers are not paying income tax simply because they are not earning sufficient income.
A suggestion I would like to make is this. Looking into the future, I think what ought to be done is to endeavour to eliminate waste. During the years that have passed many blunders have been made. Going back as far as 1912, I think a gigantic blunder was made when the Welland canal was started. The first estimate of cost made by the engineers on this work was $50,000,000, but it has already cost more than $62,000,000, and the last estimate of the engineers is that the cost will reach $114,500,000. This with interest will bring the cost when completed to approximately $140,000,000. If you take a pencil and reckon the interest on that at four per cent you find that it amounts to $5,600,000 a year. This canal was built ostensibly for the three prairie provinces. We will suppose, just for the sake of getting an approximate reckoning, that each province pays its share of the interest. That would leave one-third, or $1,866,000 to be paid by the three prairie provinces in interest alone. In view of that charge, where are they going to make a gain after the Welland canal is completed? All the benefit they will get from the completion of the canal is that the larger ships carrying their grain will be able to go through the Welland canal, and about 150 miles further. If they save one cent a bushel -I think that is about the highest estimate one can make-and if 100,000,000 bushels passed down the canal each year, which I think is about the most we have reason to expect will pass eastward, that will mean a saving of $1,000,000 a year, so that the benefit to the three prairie provinces would be less than their share of the interest. If that is the case with the three prairie provinces, for whose benefit the canal was supposed in the main to be built, what is to be the experience of Ontario? What is to be the experience of Quebec? What is to be the experience of the maritime provinces and of British Columbia? I think a very great mistake was made in starting to build the Welland canal. We do not get any benefit from it until we have invested $114,000,000, and I, omitted to mention that the interest on that would amount to probably $20,000,000, making a total of approximately $140,000,000.
Let me mention some other mistakes we have made in the past. We are considering at the present time various huge projects involving a large expenditure of money, such

The Budget-Mr. Millar
as the St. Lawrence waterway development, the building of the Georgian bay canal, and other enterprises, and in view of that I thought it might not be out of the way to refer back to some of the mistakes that have been made in the past. I have already mentioned the Welland canal.
The second mistake was the building of paralleling railway lines-wasteful duplication. We have in western Canada, and in some places in eastern Canada, railway lines paralleling each other for fifty, sixty or a hundred miles, only a mile to three miles apart, while in other districts the people are drawing their grain long distances to the railroad, in some cases doing their marketing forty miles away. That was one blunder for which we are paying dearly now.
Another costly error was the building at enormous cost of the National Transcontinental to Quebec, and then the raising of freight rates to such an extent that very little freight travels on that line. If hon. members would refer to the arguments advanced at that time they would see that the road was built to carry our grain to Quebec, to keep it in Canadian channels. For a short time after the road was built the rate was low, six cents a bushel, but I believe it is now about twenty-one cents. The result is that after an expenditure of hundreds of millions of dollars the railway is not used for the purpose for which it was built. Hon. members may think lightly of that, but as a matter of fact Canada is paying for that blunder.

but after thinking it over, I believe it is quite to the point to draw to the attention
3264D-50
of hon. members what may be gained by watchfulness in this House. We sit here day by day and sometimes appear to take matters lightly, but there is a great amount of work being done, and large saving can be made by hon. members if they are watching. I am going to mention two circumstances. In 1923 Mr. Wallace, a member of the Progressive group and an electrical engineer, rose when the then hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George proposed a private bill for the renewing of a patent, and opposed the measure. I do not think there was another member in this House who knew there was anything dangerous being put through, and I do not think the member for St. Lawrence-St. George knew it himself. He probably had been requested to put this private bill through and was proceeding to do it. Mr. Wallace, whose constituency I have forgotten-

speechtext: Elgin.

speechtext:
-arose in his .place and in a twenty minute speech saved to this country $15,000,000 in six years. It was done in this way: He pointed out that this company had received a charter in Great Britain in about 1904, a charter in the United States about 1906 and one in Canada about the same year. They enjoyed the privilege in one country for seventeen years and in another country a little less, and they had applied in Great Britain to have the patent renewed and had been refused. They had applied in the United States, and had been refused, and this time they were before the Canadian parliament. It was all new to us. He pointed out that during the time they were protected in their patent, the price of a little tube used in the radio was $9, then it dropped to $6, and after the expiration of the patent it dropped to $4. He said, "I believe that if this patent is renewed for seven years"-that was the time asked for-"the price will rise $2 on * each tube." An estimate was made of the number of tubes used in Canada, and it figured out $15,060,000 in six years-one year had then expired. That is just one example of what can be saved by watchfulness. Probably not one person in Canada out of a thousand knew that this saving had been made, or how it was made, or anything about it.
I desire to refer to another instance. Those who sat in this House in 1921 will remember that a request was made for the renewal of a coal lease in Alberta which was known as the Hoppe Isenberg lease. I am not going fully into the details of it, but that bill passed through the House and everybody seemed to take it as a matter of fact. It went to the Senate and was checked up there. A confer-

The Budget-Mr. Millar

ertce took place between members of the Senate and members of the House of Commons, and the lease was refused. A later discussion in this House revealed the fact that the lease of that property, if my memory serves me rightly, was worth from two hundred million to three hundred million dollars. I believe the then leader of the opposition, Right Hon. Arthur Meighen, made the statement that a provisional sale had been made to English capitalists for that amount. That shows the importance of watchfulness and care.
I desire to make another suggestion. We have been discussing the tariff, and sometimes one is a little in doubt-I frankly confess that at times I am in doubt-whether we will ever be able to reach the point where we can do away entirely with the tariff, and, if you will, with protection. What I believe should be done is to lower the tariff all round, because it is a great inconvenience-injustice is the word I wanted to use-to those manufacturing in one line if the protection they enjoy is removed while other products are protected. It places them in the same position as that in which the farmer finds himself at the present time. The Canadian farmer cannot be protected, but he must buy in a protected market. If after we have thoroughly studied this matter, and after the data has been received from the tariff board, those of us who believe we should eventually have free trade 'find we must compromise with other parts of Canada, that we must carry a certain part of the burden of the cost of that protective tariff, then I think even in western Canada we could do so, provided the government would do more to help us in connection with agriculture.
Let me give hon. gentlemen some figures to show what has been the result of this assistance the government has already given. They have - been fostering agriculture in all its branches. I need only refer to what has been done in the way of growing earlier and stronger varieties of wheat. Marquis wheat has revolutionized the industry in the west and is now being used largely in the United States and even in South America. Where would Canada be to-day as a wheat growing country but for that fostering care on the part of the government? No individual farmer could do that experimenting himself, for it is expensive work; but as a result of the assistance of the government we are very well to the front in the wheat growing industry. Perhaps it would be surprising to some if I were to say, what is a fact, that in sixteen years at the Chicago exposition Canada won the grand championship in wheat fourteen times. In the

forefront among the provinces is Saskatchewan, but we are pleased to see that our sister province of Alberta has won the championship in the last two years; and as wheat growing is moving westward and northward, Alberta will probably become the banner wheat province of Canada.
What about oats? Twelve times out of sixteen Canada has taken the grand championship for oats at Chicago, and when it comes to another department of agriculture, horses, in nine years the Clvesdale horses of Canada have taken thirty championships at Chicago. There will come a time when we will ask for greater assistance for agriculture, and I point out these Canadian successes in order to show that the money ls by no means wasted. Canada would not occupy the position she does to-day in regard to grain, cattle, hogs and poultry if it were not for the fostering care of the Canadian government. Perhaps the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Motherwell) may suggest that I am overlooking the fact thatlthe business of production is really a provincial matter. I do not forget that fact, but I have in mind also that while that is true the Dominion government has been doing a considerable amount of work along this line and there is no reason why it should not continue to do so.
We are sometimes advised to take up mixed farming in the west. In order that hon. gentlemen who have not had the privilege of visiting that part of Canada, and Who therefore are not familiar with western conditions, may learn something about the west, I want to point out that we are rapidly following this advice. We are going into mixed farming more 3nd more. I will give you the figures for Manitoba, and I take that province because it is in the lead in taking up mixed farming. You will be surprised to know that the wheat acreage in 1903 and the wheat acreage in 1926 were just about the same in Manitoba. But what about other industries? In four points in Manitoba they are shipping honey by the carload, and from forty to forty-eight per cent of the barley grown in Canada is produced in Manitoba. Last year that province produced $450,000 worth of turkeys while the vegetable crop in 1926 totalled $3,000,000 exclusive of potatoes. Here are some interesting figures: agricultural products in 1917, 1918 and 1919 in that province, amounted to $2,000,000; in the following three years they fell to $100,000,000 and in the next succeeding three years tiny went up 'to $150,000,000.
I intend to touch on one more matter before I sit down. I will pick out one department and discuss it in detail in order to show what progress is possible, and I am taking,

The Budget-Mr. Millar
not the grain industry, not cattle, horses, piga and sheep, but one of the smaller activities. I do this for two reasons: first, because it has been most neglected, and secondly, because we are going to hold a poultry congress in Ottawa this coming summer. The industry to which I refer is of course poultry raising. It may seem like a small thing, but as a matter of fact it is not. One gathers a dozen eggs here and a dozen there, and this may appear insignificant. But when it is pointed out that the egg production of Canada in 1926 represented the sum of $66,000,000, and this from the farms alone, you will see that the industry is of some magnitude. Here is a remarkable fact about the poultry industry: Canada does not produce sufficient eggs to supply her own market. We exported in 1926 2,501,000 dozen eggs and imported 3,341,000 dozen. It is only some eight or ten years ago that the government of Canada took any serious steps towards improving the poultry industry. Now see where Canada stands in this regard. A year ago I listened to an address by a gentleman who stands at the head of the poultry work at the experimental farm and I heard him make this statement. He said, "we thought at one time that Canada's cold climate was a handicap to the poultry industry of the country, but instead of that it has proved an asset." This man took pens of poultry over , to Spain last j'ear and of twenty-five countries represented the Canadian exhibit stood up best, surprising the poultry raisers from abroad. Sixty-four countries hold egg-laying contests, and there is an opportunity of bringing them together and making comparisons between the achievements of Canadian hens and those of other countries. What has been the result? In 1925, out of 64 countries in which these contests are held, 39 hens laid 300 eggs or more each in one year, and of those 39 hens 19 were from Canada. Is not that a record? In 1926 the results were equally good. The pen that took the lead was also Canadian, giving an average of 296 eggs, while one Canadian hen laid the largest number of eggs of any bird recorded in any country since contests have been known-351 eggs. We do not know what hens may have done of which there is no record, but of those of which any record has been kept the Canadian hens have been foremost. The hen that laid these 351 eggs was owned by the university of British Columbia. The eggs from that hen are selling to-day not for 25 cents each but for $25 each, and the demand cannot be supplied. During that year that hen laid her weight in eggs each month, approximately.

I would like to say a word about the poultry congress before taking my seat. This year this congress is to be held in Ottawa; forty countries will be represented, and I fear that unless it receives more publicity and encouragement the benefit to our poultry industry and the advertising Canada may get from it will be lost. Last year this congress was held in Spain and there was a great fight between Canada and the United States to secure the meeting for this year; Canada won, and Ottawa has been chosen as the place of meeting. There will be present 8,000 delegates; on the program will be representatives from Japan, Russia, Germany, France and Persia, as well as a large number from the United States, from which country I believe 3,000 delegates are coming. This is a wonderful opportunity to advertise Canada. Why are they coming to this country? They are coming here because Canada has taken the lead in the poultry industry, and it has taken that lead simply because it has been given encouragement by the government. One of our representatives addressed a gathering in New Jersey some time ago; that state is well in advance in the poultry industry, and after his address was finished the gentleman at the head of that industry in New Jersey said, "Everything we have done in this state has been copied from Canada." Canada is now looked upon by the poultry raisers of other countries as the country which will supply the breeding stock of the future, because of our registration system, which I have not had time to deal with. It just comes to my mind now that recently a gentleman in Ontario sold a bird to someone in the United States for $125.
In order to point out just what progress is possible in this industry let me say that the poultry branch discovered that by mating one breed of laying hens with an excellent laying strain they were able to increase the egg production by forty per cent in one season. A short time ago I had occasion to go into the poultry department of the experimental farm near my home. It was thought that the cold in that part of the country would be such that the hens would not lay during the winter, but there I found that a pen of 95 pullets were laying 60 eggs per day with the thermometer between 40 and 47 below zero. So there is no reason why enormous strides should not be made in this industry. We have talked sometimes of subsidizing industries. We on this side of the House are not much in favour of that, but here is a way in which the agricultural industry could be assisted and enabled to lighten the farmers' burden. I think it would

be well if, when grants are asked for agricultural purposes, those who are engaged in manufacturing and as merchants were very-generous in these expenditures.

In closing may I say that we who reside in the western provinces and who are engaged in farming are sometimes urged to be broadminded and to look at things from a national viewpoint. So far as I am concerned, and I believe others take the same attitude, I realize that there is a place in Canada for industries, and we do not want to crush them out. All we ask is that we have a fair chance also. Together we can develop Canada; together we should endeavour to strengthen the weak spots which are continually being found. The maritime provinces will and no doubt should receive some assistance, and it is well that we should take a national view in considering all parts of Canada. We ask no protection as growers of grain or stock but an opportunity to make a fair living; we do not want to carry the burdens of others and neither do we desire to load our burdens on anyone else. We are willing to listen to those from, other parts of Canada who are engaged in industries of which we know little; we can learn from them and we want to understand them; we want to do the fair thing and to be generous when they ask for assistance, but we do ask the same consideration from other partis of Canada.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the observations I shall make at this time will be much more brief than I had at one time intended; the debate is dragging along and I do not think it would be wise to take a very great deal of time now.
As I approach a discussion of the budget proposals let me say that I feel something like the Scotchman who was going to get married. As the time for the ceremony drew near it was observed that he was looking somewhat downcast, and he was asked by a friend if he had lost the ring. To this he replied, " No, but I have lost my enthusiasm." I say very frankly, Mr. Speaker, that I do not accept the budget as presented with a great deal of enthusiasm. In its two major parts, those re-
IMr. Millar.]
ferring to the tariff and to the reduction in the income tax, it is not my idea of what a budget should be. The reduction in the income tax, in so far as that might seem to indicate the intention or the disposition to further reduction with a view to the total elimination of the tax, meets with my entire disapproval.
The tariff has been discussed year after year, session after session, and it would seem to be maintained by some that there is no difference between those on different sides of the House. The hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Guthrie) in an address this afternoon that was listened to, I am sure, with a great deal of interest by every person in the House-and the hon. gentleman is to be congratulated upon the way in which that speech was delivered, in spite of the fact that as he proceeded we could here and there detect fallacies in the argument-maintained that the Conservative party is not a high tariff party. I think, however, we have reason to suspect that it is at least a higher tariff party. During the course of the election campaign I got hold of a certain document which I do not think was intended by those who circulated it to get into the hands of the antiConservative candidates. However, I got it; it was given to me by one of the retail merchants in my constituency. It was a circular letter issued by Bates and Innes of Garleton Place who, I understand, have close relations with the Hawthorne Woollen Mills. The Hawthorne Woollen Mills, which were the subject of discussion some two or three years ago, are located, as those of you who were here then will remember, in Carleton Place, a short distance from Ottawa. In this circular letter there were three interesting paragraphs. One was to the effect that a protectionist government was going to be elected. That was a prophecy and, as it proved, a false one. It went on to urge the argument upon the retail merchants that when this protectionist government came in the tariff would be increased, that in consequence of the tariff prices would be higher-that was the effect of the argument-and consequently they urged upon customers that this would be a good time to buy. I think you may be sure, Mr. Speaker, that I did not neglect to make use of that circular letter in the course of my election campaign in trying to prove that hon. gentlemen opposite were in favour at least of a higher tariff, if not what they are pleased to call a high tariff. That I think affords us some justification for at least trying to distinguish between the two.
I may say frankly in regard to the income tax that there are some respects in which I

The Budget-Mr. Brown
recognize that there are anomalies. Is there any system of taxation that has been or can be proposed that can meet all the requirements laid down by Adam Smith, or those who have sought to add to the principles which he has formulated? There is no system of taxation that can be applied with absolute equity. We recognize some anomalies in the income tax system. I listened with a good deal of interest to the argument put forward by the member for St. Antoine (Mr. Bell) this evening; it is a speech worthy of the consideration of every member of the House. But speaking generally the income tax, to my mind, is the fairest tax in principle, for the principle of it is that it is levied upon those who are able to bear the burden. Now, as I have said, there may be anomalies in its application; there may be inconsistencies; at times it may not be equitably applied, but in principle the tax is sound.
Unfortunately we have in politics, as we have in theology, men who are not able to distinguish between fundamentals and incidentals, and the evils or the anomalies of the income tax are incidentals. The principle is that men shall bear the burden in proportion to their ability to bear it, and that is a principle which we must maintain. That principle does not hold in connection with the customs tariff tax, or in connection with the proposal of the hon. member for West Calgary (Mr. Bennett), a tax on turnovers. Those taxes are laid not upon those who are best able to bear the burden but upon those who cannnot escape from the burden and must bear it. You will remember that the hon. member for Fort William (Mr. Manion) a year ago introduced into the debate a hypothetical widow who was getting an income of three or four thousand dollars a year from shares that her husband had left her, and he professed great sympathy for women in that position. I also have sympathy with widows, but I have a good deal more sympathy for the widow who has to rear a family of children and provide them with food and clothing, and has not the amount of income on which she can claim exemption-a good deal more sympathy for those who are placed in that position.
I submit, Mr. -Speaker, that though in some respects the income tax as applied may be open to objection, it is in principle the fairest tax that we have. The objection is raised that it is not fair because the farmers do not pay it. Well, they do not pay it, as has been asserted again and again, because they have not the income upon which to pay. I know it is hard to convince hon. members opposite, some of them at least, that the farmer is not
in a position to pay his income tax. One hon. member opposite made a remark about the 400,000,000 bushels of wheat that was raised in the west. Four hundred million bushels of wheat is an immense amount, but those who are acquainted with the facts know that the overhead cost of raising that wheat is enormous, and that the amount in the hands of the farmer after he has paid all the costs is a very small proportion of what that wheat brought upon the world's markets.
The hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Cahan) seemed to be under some misapprehension in regard to the farmer and the income tax, but I want to point out to him one feature that he did not consider, and it ds this: the place of the farm woman in the production of revenue. The hon. member for Qu'Appelle (Mr. Millar) has been dealing with the poultry industry. He referred to the fact that some $450,000 worth of turkeys had been raised in Manitoba during the last year. I believe the total amount of poultry produced in Manitoba during the year 1926 would run very close to $5,000,000. That amount of wealth, Mr. Speaker, was contributed to Canada by the work of the women, in very large measure, and when we farmers make our returns to the income tax branch we are not allowed to take account of the work that ds done by the women-it all goes into the one pot. I want to say further that the woman on the farm is doing much more in contributing to the wealth of the country than the woman in other walks of life. I am not speaking of those women who are engaged in industry, I am not speaking of the wives of those men who are in a position to claim an exemption, we will say, to the extent of $3,000. Those women may be doing their work and doing it well. I have no criticism to make against what they they are doing, but they are not contributing to the wealth of the country in the same way that the farmers' wives are contributing. The latter are doing the work of their household just as other women are doing it, and besides, they are adding to the wealth of the country; yet there is no recognition of that when we make our income tax returns. That is a feature that I think ought to be considered by the hon. member for St. Uawrence-St. George, and I think it is a feature that has been very frequently overlooked.
The hon. member for Toronto West Centre (Mr. Hocken) had something to say on this question. He spoke of the farmers of the United States being protectionists, and instanced the McNary-Haugen bill as a proof
The Budget-Mr. Brown

of that fact. The hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Garland), commenting on that statement, said that the McNary-Haugen bill is a bribe of the -worst type; that it is a bribe to agriculturists in the United States to accept protection; it cannot be interpreted as anything else-a bribe of the worst type, and the farmers there will suffer for it if they accept it. I do not take exception to what was said by the hon. member for Bow River, but I should like to put it in another form. The McNary-Haugen bill, which has been vetoed by the President in the last few days, was the result of the conviction that had grown up in the minds of the United States farmers that they could not be benefited by a protective tariff. They had for many years been deceived by a sham tariff; they found out that it was giving them no real protection, and they came foiward with the demand that they should be given real protection in the shape of the McNary

Haugen bill just as the other industries were given protection. What did they meet with? They met with the most intense opposition from the interests which had benefited by protection. It was said to them: Oh, but if that bill passes, then the cost of living will go up. The cost of manufacture will go up and we will not be able to compete in the markets of the world. So the cost of living would go up and the farmers would not find themselves in any better position than they were in before. In the interest of the experiment I would perhaps like to have seen the McNary-Haugen bill tried out, but on the other hand in the interests of sound economics, it is well that the President of the United States saw fit to veto it.
I have been amazed at some of the fallacies to which utterance has been given during the debate by some hon. members opposite, from the first hon. member who spoke, the hon. member for West Calgary (Mr. Bennett), almost down to the last. It was urged upon us that taxation had not been reduced and elaborate figures were produced to show that such was the case. Large numbers of percentages of taxation were brought to our notice. The one thing that hon. members seem to forget-and this is the fallacy that runs all through their arguments-is that a reduction in the rate of taxation does not necessarily mean a reduction in the total revenue. So long as our revenue is raised by a system of indirect taxation by a tax on the goods that we consume, just so long will it be impossible for any government to determine exactly what the revenue will be at the end of any year. All that any government can do is to fix the rate of taxation and LMr. Brown.]
to estimate on the basis of the last year's business that the revenue will be so and so. Therefore all that any government can do is to reduce the rate of taxation. When we went before tariff commissions, we used to uige a reduction in the tariff and we would be met by the Objection: Yes, but where are you going to get the revenue? We would give the very obvious retort that it was quite possible to reduce the tariff and yet increase the revenue. Nevertheless hon. gentlemen opposite have not been able to grasp that very simple proposition and the fallacy appears all through the debate.
Let me give an illustration of that. A good deal has been said about the reduction in the duty on automobiles, and it has even been urged that the taxation on the people has been increased by the action of the government last session. W'hat are the facts? More was collected in customs duties during the nine months ended December 31, 1926, than during the corresponding period in the previous year. I will give the House the figures From April 1 to December 31, 1925, there were imported into Canada 853 commercial trucks at a value of $1,245,654 and the duty collected amounted to $429,392. During the corresponding period in 1926 there were imported 1,863 commercial trucks at a value of $2,291,674, and the duty collected amounted to $447,951. That is. the number of cars more than doubled; the duty was lower, but there was an increase in the total revenue in that particular line of cars of more than $20,000.
Let me doal now with the question of percentages. I am speaking of the nine-month period, because we have not yet had a whole year under which the new duties have been in force, and indeed it should be said that only part of the nine-month period was under the lower scale of duty. In the nine months ended December 31, 1925, there were imported 11,494 passenger cars at a value of $10,847,171, and the duty collected amounted to $3,776,665. In 1926 for -the same nine-month period, 22,904 cars were imported, or practically double the number, at a value of $18,387,615, and the duty collected amounted to $4,346,869, or an increase in customs revenue from the importation of cars of $570,204. According to the logic of hon. gentlemen opposite the government increased taxation upon those cars because, as they argued, the total revenue from that trade was increased by $570,204. Yet the fact is-we well know it and every person throughout -the country will -testify to it-that a car could be bought cheaper during that period than during the {corresponding period of the preceding year. These are facts of which the

Hie Budget-Mr. Brown
public is well aware, and yet hon. members opposite will confuse the issue by these fallacies.
The same is true in regard to the references made by the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens) to percentages of duty, the taxation being higher at one time than at another, because the percentage of the tariff was higher. When I heard the hon. member speaking of percentages in that way, I was reminded of the story of the darky porter. A traveller asked him what was the average tip that was given to him by people who travelled with him. The darky said: "A dollar". Well, the man wanted to be up to the average and so he handed the porter a dollar. "Thank you, sir," said the darky, "thank you, you are the first man that has come up to the average." Here again the same fallacy creeps in. There is nothing more midleading than averages. When we talk about average duties, we must remember that they will vary as the amount of free goods varies with the amount of taxable goods, and according as the amount coming in under a high duty varies in relation to that coming in under a low duty. One is almost ashamed to give utterance to platitudes and to discuss these very obvious things, but one is forced to do it.
Let us suppose that we have coming in $1,000 worth of free goods and $1,000 worth of dutiable goods, bearing twenty-five per cent. The revenue collected from that $2,000 worth of imports will be $250. Let us suppose that the next year there is still only $1,000 worth of free goods coming in, and that the duty on the dutiable goods has been reduced to twenty per cent. It would be quite possible to show by the change from one figure to another that the average on the whole had been increased, and yet the fallacy there is perfectly evident. I do not pretend, Mr. Speaker, to be an expert accountant. There are some realms into which I would not presume to enter, but when I hear hon. gentlemen giving utterance to these very obvious fallacies, though I would not presume to have any expert opinion, I cannot allow them to pass unchallenged.
The hon. member for Frontenac-Addington (Mr. Edwards) also I think merits a little attention. He gave us one of his characteristic speeches last night, in the course of which he referred to the reciprocity pact of 1911. He wanted to know if any member on this side of the House would put that pact into force if he had the power to do it. He was not satisfied to take an answer from private
members, and finally he got his answer from some members of the cabinet. Then he pointed out that in that pact provision was made for certain duties on certain lines of machinery, and then he asked: Would you put those rates into force to-day? I went to the library to-day to look at the pamphlet containing the terms of that pact, and I find that while the hon. member stated the facts correctly, his inferences were all wrong. It is true that the duties were as he stated, but there was nothing in that pact that would render it obligatory upon Canada to maintain those duties at those rates. Those were maximum rates, not minimum rates. The theory of the protectionist is that it is a bad thing for us to import goods, that we are doing a particular favour to our neighbour when we lower the tariff against his goods. In view of that theory held by protectionists, is it not absurd for the hon. member for Frontenac-Addington to say that we would be under any obligation to maintain the tariff on these imports at the rates that were agreed upon by those who devised the reciprocity pact? Were we to put that agreement into force to-day there would be absolutely nothing in it that would require us to raise our tariff on this list of imports to the level of the United States tariff. The whole argument as advanced by the hon. member was, like some of the: other arguments, so absurd that it is not worthy of serious consideration.
There are many things that I might have said, Mr. Speaker, but I shall forbear at this time. The natural question is: How do we regard this budget, speaking of it in general terms? I have said already that we have no particular enthusiasm for the budget in itself. While the answer given by the Minister of Railways (Mr. Dunning) to the hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Glen) is by no means as plain and specific as we would desire, yet we feel that we have possibly no warrant for assuming that the action taken in the Robb budget of 1926 is the last step to ]pe taken in the direction of lower tariffs. On the contrary, we would like to assume that the minister intended to convey to us the idea that there was still to be a progress in that direction. That impression is, of course, confirmed by the statement of the Finance minister this afternoon, that the present government is a low tariff government, and is proud of it. With that in mind, Mr. Speaker, we have felt that we can give our support to the budget, notwithstanding the fact that in itself there is nothing that arouses any particular enthusiasm. I would like to add
792	COMMONS
The Budget-Mr. McLean (Meljort)
that the Minister of Finance must not assume that any support we may give the present budget will warrant his concluding that if next year's budget should not show some further inclination to go in the direction of the principles we have advocated, our support will be continued.
I do not know, Mr. Speaker, that I have anything further to say at this time. The hour is rapidly approaching when we are likely to take a vote, and in view of that fact I shall give way to those who are to follow.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hour is getting late and I do not intend to take up very much time, but there are a few things I wish to say before a vote is taken.
In the first place, I think this House will agree with me that this is a budget to which there is no real, strong, sustained opposition. On the other hand, it may be that it does not arouse in some of us the enthusiasm that last year's budget did, but I think that throughout the country, from coast to coast, it has been received with a good deal of satisfaction. I have received many letters from western Canada, from my own constituency in particular, and in them there has been no word of disapproval or of criticism of the budget as it is. That is sometimes as a fair test of a budget, as it is of the work of a government official in any office when there is no great enthusiasm about what he does and no great objection to what he does. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) is to be congratulated that he has under all the circumstances produced a balance sheet such as the one we have before us.
There is one thing I do know, Sir, and that is that the people of Canada are able to-day to congratulate themselves upon having emerged from the position they were in five years ago to a much higher and safer ground financially. This budget is of value and is satisfactory to the country because it shows ah undoubted financial strength. It is satisfactory because of the psychological effect of the reduction in the national debt. That is something worth while not only in Canada, but throughout other parts of the empire and other countries of the world, particularly those from which we expect in the future to get immigrants to fill our vacant spaces and develop the resources of this Dominion. We heard a great deal about immigration to-day from the hon. leader of the apposition (Mr. Guthrie). I would remind you, Sir, and this House, that five years ago it was pretty hard to find anyone here advocating that the gov-
IMr. Brown.]
ernment should hasten the work of encouraging immigrants to come to Canada. The sentiment against encouraging immigration has died down to a great extent since then, although it is not altogether extinct. But the fact that Canada is reducing its debt and its taxation, that Canada's financial position has been strengthened, and that employment is better, will help to bring to our shores the immigrants that we need.
I said a moment ago that this budget does not arouse in some of us the enthusiasm that the last budget did. A critic of the budget said the other day that it is referred to as the Robb budget, and he qualified that by saying that he did not use the word in the sense of r-o-b. I wish to tell hon. gentlemen that some of his friends were not so particular; they were fond of calling it a "rob" budget instead of the proper name, but the people of Canada did not pay much attention to that. After going home last year we found that the budget had occasioned great enthusiasm throughout the country. I found in western Canada that possibly the budget had a good deal to do with the progress being made in that country at the time. In nearly a quarter of a century in the west I had not seen so much new land cleared and broken and being got ready for crop in any one year, and I had never seen so many people flocking into the north country, so much new building in the towns and rural districts, and so much genuine progress in that part of the country with which I am most familiar.
I am glad that to-day we do not hear very much of the pessimistic talk we heard last year. I am not going to refer to it now because it would be unkind to do so. After the last election a good friend of mine said to me, "If you had power to inflict some punishment upon your opponents in the last election, what is the worst thing you could think of?" I said I did not feel inclined to do anything. He said, the worst thing * you could do would be to ask them to read their speeches of last session in parliament, and I would not consider doing that. There is reasonable prosperity in Canada everywhere to-day, not perhaps as much as the people would like, but as compared with any other country there is reasonable prosperity. That did not come about solely on account of the good crop of last year. It came about as a result of careful work on the part of the producers for the past five years, and as a result of the extent to which the government took care of the financial resources of the country. But it is not all due to the past year. We are told that last year the crop was one of the largest on record.

The Budget-Mr. McLean (Meljort)
Well, it was a fair crop but not particularly large. Last year Canada produced 406,000,000 bushels of wheat as against 411,000,000 bushels the year before. The figures are as follows: the total yield of wheat in Canada for the year 1926 is estimated at 406,269,000 bushels from 22,768,449 acres, as compared with 411,375,700 bushels from 21,972,732 acres in 1925 and with 386,864,525 bushels from 22,084,320 acres, the annual averages for the four years 1922-25. When it comes to oats we find the crop amounted in 1926 to only 404,000,000 bushels as against 513,000,000 bushels in 1925, and an average of 493,000,000 bushels in the four years. So that it was not entirely due to the good crop last year, because we had crops just as good previously, and sometimes a little better, and we had not the same prosperity in the country. Other products, such as pulp and paper, forest products, and the products of the mine and the waters had a great deal to do with the restoration of prosperity. The farmers of western Canada I am sure were helped by the crop of 1925. The crop of 1926 was a fair one and the prices received were also fair, but the crop was harvested under tremendous difficulties, and still the 1926 crop helped the country somewhat further on the way to better times.
In the past we have been told a great deal of the wonderful wealth in the country to the south of us. Some of us have been of the opinion that those gentlemen, whether they were hon. members of this House or outside of this House, who continuously told of the prosperity of the United States on account of higher tariff protection were not doing a service to Canada. I find that the great country to the south of us is not uniformly prosperous and is not growing very fast in population in certain states.
Referring to the statement of the hon. leader of the opposition that the prairie provinces had not increased in population in the last few years as much as they might have, I desire to read an item in an American paper which says:
The Borough of Queens, one of the five divisions of greater New York, having doubled its population in the last six years-
Very encouraging, but it is the city population that has doubled in that time.
-this means that 483,000 persons have settled in Queens since January 1, 1921. The growth in population of this one section of New York in that short period is greater than the population of many a state. At the last census, there were nine states-Arizona, Delaware, Idaho, Nevada, New Hampshire, New Mexico, Utah, Vermont and Wyoming-each of which had a population of less than 483,000. Delaware. Nevada and AVyoming all together have less than that number.
Nine states in that rich country, each of them with a population less than that of any one of eight provinces in the Dominion!
I have some figures which I am going to give to Hansard dealing with the question of prices of farm implements. I had thought that the discussion in regard to the price of implements in 1924 and other years had come to an end, and I was surprised to hear the leader of the opposition, in that otherwise very admirable speech, give us some figures on farm implements to show that prices had increased as a result of tariff reductions. I hold in my hand a statement with regard to the prices of implements sold by the International Harvester Company, dated October 16, 1925, showing prices of Deering and McCormick machinery at that time. The figures are as follows:

Last year in Saskatchewan we did not have to discuss any of these figures during the general election, because the people of that province were satisfied that the steps taken by the government had been in the right direction; and they expect confidently-and I am sure they will not be disappointed-that further steps along the same lines will be taken in due course.

speechtext:
I have not the figures. I think the hon. member for Mackenzie would be in a better position to supply the information. I am prepared to take his word for it that reductions were made prior to that time. When the policy of the government cutting the tariff on such implements was introduced, we remember the wail that went up from hon. members in this House about the ruination of the agricultural implement industry. I am glad my hon. friend asked me that question, because it reminds me that a few days ago we read in the newspapers about the great rise in value of the stock of a Canadian implement company, sale prices running up to $110 a share. This stock a few years ago was worth between $50 and $60. I am not sure of the exact figures,
794	COMMONS
The Budget-Mr. McLean (Melfort)
and I do not want to exaggerate, but it was a low figure a few years ago. They made those reductions; they stood for the cut in the tariff, and the farmers were placed in a better position to patronize them than they had been previously.
I wish to devote a little time to a speech delivered in this House last Friday evening and which in my opinion was very unfair in some respects. The speech referred to was delivered by the bon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens), and I am glad to see him in his place to-night. To my mind it was studded with unfair statements-probably worse than that, but we will come to that point later. The first thing I take exception to in this speech is the propagating of the idea that, the budget having come down so early, the people of this country have been more or less relieved of their apprehension lest the tariff be reduced. The hon. member referred to the statement of the Bank of Montreal in their official bulletin of February 23, as follows:
The early delivery of the budget speech by the Dominion Minister of Finance, and the announcement that no tariff changes are to be made, should be helpful to business by removing that uncertainty and hesitancy in mercantile transactions which sometimes wait upon the late pronouncement of government fiscal policy.
I agree with the bank in that regard, but I do not think that, rightly understood, the statement necessarily conveys the meaning which the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens) apparently was anxious to infer from it. He seemed to suppose that there was some fear that there would be reductions in the customs tariff, whereas it is just as likely that the country might be afraid that a long delayed budget statement might propose increases in that direction.
I come to the next point on which I disagree with the hon. gentleman. I will quote his own words:
Yes, the budget was welcomed for what it did not do, not for anything that it did. We welcome it in so far as in it the government has stayed its hand in further reductions of the tariff. The government announces

This is the point I want to emphasize.
-in the budget that it is not its intention this year utterly to destroy the remaining fragment of a protective principle in the tariff.
Yet further on in the same address the hon. gentleman tells us that there has been no change in the tariff; it is the same as it was before. Here is what he says:
There is exactly the same protection in the tariff to-day as there was prior to 1921; in fact a little more.
[Mr. McI.ean.1
I will go beyond the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens) and quote the words of one who, many of us regret, is not with us to-night, the late leader of the opposition, Mr. Meighen. Let me quote what he had to say last year. Of course, there was an election at that time and he was appealing to the people for support, as we all do. Speaking at Owen-tSound on September 8, he is reported as follows:
He pressed his tariff views, declaring his intention to revise the tariff basis of protection. The principle governing every schedule of the tariff would be the principle of protection. "That is the principle," he declared, "we intend to restablish in our country".
If it had not been disestablished how could it be reestablished? However, I will not press that point. I will now consider some of the financial criticisms of the budget. I would not have undertaken to discuss the budget from this standpoint because I do not profess to be a skilled accountant, but as I listened to the speech of the hon. member for Vancouver Centre the other night it occurred to me that he made certain statements which obviously were altogether erroneous. In particular he made a statement to which I shall refer later on regarding the resources of Saskatchewan, a statement so utterly absurd to me that I got the hon. gentleman's speech next day in Hansard and read it carefully to make sure that I had followed him. The more carefully I read that speech the greater the number of absurdities I discovered in it, and therefore decided to devote some time to a fuller consideration of it. Discussing the public debt the hon. member, after declaring that he was not criticising the Minister of Finance personally, made the following statement:
On April 10, 1924, he said our surplus would be $20,750,000, to be applied to the reduction of the public debt. On March 24, 1925, he said that the public debt had been decreased by $35,900,000. On April 15, 1926, the minister informed the House, there had been a reduction in the debt of $22,350,000. On February 17, 1927, at page 387 of Hansard the minister made the statement that there would be a reduction of $31,000,000 in our debt. The individual reductions indicated in these four announcements total $110,000,000 so that there should be a reduction in the debt to that extent from the year 1922.
The hon. member then goes on to complain that there is no evidence of that $110,000,000 of a reduction. On the next page of the report of his speech he refers to the funded debt. He finds that the funded debt at the present time amounts to $2,471,000,000. Then he sets out the difference between the funded

The Budget-Mr. McLean (Meljort)
debt and the net debt. The net debt on March 31, 1922, according to the hon. gentleman, was $2,422,000,000, and on December 31, 1926, including the amount paid off last fall it was $2,343,000,000. To quote his words:
That is to say, we have a reduction in the net debt of $79,000,000 in a period of five years. That is nothing for this country to be proud of. I ask, where is the $110,000,000 of a reduction in the debt as announced by the Minister of Finance officially year by year.
I do not know whether the House or the hon. gentleman has been able to follow these quotations from the speech in question, but certainly I could not understand, nor do I understand now, what relation the $2,422,000,000 in the shape of a net debt as of March 31,
1922,	has to the funded debt of $2,471,000,000. I therefore made inquiries. I recollected that between 1922 and the year which the hon. member for Vancouver Centre took as his starting point there was another fiscal year,
1923,	and in that period there was not a surplus but a deficit which had to be added to the debt. That was a reasonable deficit and not one of which we need be ashamed1. It was not incurred during the regime of the present minister, but while his predecessor was in office. Instead however of a deficit of $91,000,000 or $92,000,000 as we had in 1921, and $S1.000.000 as in 1922, we had in 1923 a deficit of $31,000,000. As the hon. member for Vancouver Centre strove to discover where the missing milions were, I thought this must be the money he had in mind. As he progressed' in his speech and linked up the $2,422,000,000 of a net debt with the funded debt of $2,471,000,000 I felt it time to cry for help. Digging info one book after another, and asking those who knew more about the matter than mysellf for some explanation of the difficulty which the hon. gentleman had created. I found that on April 10, 1924, the estimated surplus for the year 1923-24 was put at $20,750,000 but that the following year it was announced in the House that the actual decrease in the net debt for that year 1923-24 was not $20,000,000 odd but $35,900,000, or $15,000,000 more than bad been estimated the year before. The following year 1924-25 there was a surplus of only $345,589. Hon. gentlemen will remember-because the country recalls it-that in the year 1924 the minister brought in the first of those budgets that have made his name famous, and the reductions of various taxes in that budget were responsible for a decline in the revenue to such an extent that there was only the surplus of $345,000 odd just mentioned. In 1926 there was an estimated reduction in the net debt for that year of $22,350,000, but time afterwards showed that estimated reduction to be actually $27,706,586. That was the reduction last year. On February 17, 1927, the estimated reduction in the net debt for the year 192627 wias placed by the minister at $31,366,260. These actual reductions totalled $95,412,029 and the various estimates in addition to the actual decreases made $110,000,000, it is quite true. But it is absurd to take the estimated surplus to-day, and six or twelve months from now add to that the actual reduction in the figures of the debt. You will notice, Mr. Speaker, that when the deficit for the year 1922-23 is deducted' from the correct figures, $64,000,000 is left, and that is the amount of the reduction in the net debt between March 1922 and the present time. So far as the present Minister of Finance is concerned, his budgets have shown a reduction in the net debt of $95,412,029.
Then we come to another set of figures, and I am going to try to keep them apart because I have already admitted that I was somewhat confused in trying to study the speech of my hon. friend. He confused the $2,422,000,000 net debt and the $2,471,000,000 funded debt, and then deducted the annual surpluses from that funded debt. What do I find here? The funded debt as of March 31, 1922, was given by the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens), as $2,420,000,000, which is so close to the amount of the net debt that one may be excused for finding difficulty in understanding what was intended. He told us that on March 31, 1926, the funded debt amounted to $2,471,000,000, an increase in four years of $51,000,000, and giving the minister credit for the amount paid off during last year, $35,000,- [DOT] 000, would leave an increase in the funded debt of $16,000,000. But what do we find? In addition to the funded debt of $2,420,791,260 on March 31, 1922, there were temporaiy loans outstanding to the extent of $144,535,000, a grand total of $2,565,326,260 due to the public. These temporary loans the colleagues of the hon. gentleman must have known to be outstanding at the time they left office. That $145,000,000 was left entirely out of the calculations of the hon. member for Vancouver Centre. On March 31, 1926, the funded debt of Canada amounted to $2,471,965,018, with temporary loans outstanding of $201,000, giving a total of $2,472,166,018, a reduction in funded debt in four years of $93,166,018. In addition to that reduction there must be added the figures quoted by the hon. member for Vancouver Centre, the reduction during 192627 amounting to $43,000,000, so that at the end of December last year the total reduction of debt as between 1922 and 1927 was $136,106,242. It would not be a fair argument to say
